texto: I feel like i'm probably going to get attacked for only giving this 3 stars because this movie is INSANELY WELL MADE, but i just didn't connect with it as much as i thought i would. The biggest thing about 1917 is obviously the one-shot style, and yeah, it's fucking impressive. The way the camera follows Schofield and Blake through the trenches, fields and destroyed villages makes you feel like you're actually waling through WW1 with them. There were definitely moments where i completely forgot about the camera and just got sucked into what was happening. And visually, this movie is ridiculous. Roger Deakins absolutely cooked. The lighting, the landscapes, the trenches, the burning buildings at night - there are so many shots where i was just thinking  "how did they even film this?" The opening section with Schofield and Blake was probably my favourite. Their friendship feels natural, and i actually cared about what happened to them. George MacKay is also really good, especially as the movie gets more intense and Schofield is basically running on fear and adrenaline. But i think that's where my problem is. I admired the filmmaking way more than i connected with the actual story. The "one continuous shot" idea is amazing technically, but sometimes it felt like the gimmick was more interesting to me than the characters. There are also quite a few moments where i could almost see the movie setting up the next impressive shot or sequence. The film is definitely at it's best when it slows down and lets you actually sit with what's happening. The scenes where Schofield is just walking through the aftermath of everything are honestly more affecting to me than some of the bigger action sequences. It makes war feel less like an epic story and more like a horrible, exhausting place that these young men have been thrown into. The final stretch was probably the closest i got to being completely invested. Watching Schofield desperately trying to to reach the soldiers while everything is falling apart around him had me properly stressed. Incredible cinematography, great performances, amazing atmosphere, but i was more impressed than emotionally destroyed. 3/5

texto: I think this is so trite and overdrawn that it took me three attempts to finish through. Beyond the technical achievements of the film, much of the experience is bogged down by pacing issues and shallow dramaturgy, thoroughly reliant on a flimsy emotional stake that simply never stuck deep enough to elevate the otherwise amazing set pieces. Formally, too, there's almost no reason to invest any interest, as it never really moves past the gimmick of a oner, nor does it have the balls to fully commit to the bit. The camera wanders around and swings past our characters, but it feels more like a cam op hitting their marks rather than a fleshed out visual direction; it simply stages the next set-piece for us to see. The only time that the camera does feel like an actual cinematic instrument was in the trenches, where the claustrophobic corridors and shifting uniformed bodies serve to juxtapose the movements our characters are making; opposite against the huddled safety of the masses, away from the high walls of the trenches, into the open air of death. I should watch Dunkirk again.

texto: Not a fan. It felt like a theme park ride. Specifically one of those dark rides at an amusement park. You're just moved from one set piece to another with a thin objective as to why you're being moved around. The whole movie felt like it was on a rail. I couldn't get past that, and given how predictable the events of the movie are, it wasn't an exciting ride. I felt it mostly had to do with the continuous take mechanism. Its the dominating trait of the movie, and much like Rope, its an impressive process and the cuts are cleverly hidden. I can't imagine how many things had to go right for the end product to look this seamless. And to see the camera somehow keep up no matter what scene its in was cool. It's great cinematography, it shined the most in the burning village halfway into the movie. And the technical work behind the movie is still impressive: the expansive & detailed sets, as well as the huge number of extras (epic in scale, but for a simple 1hr50 movie!). But beyond that, I couldn't find anything noteworthy about the movie. Once you see what the movie is trying to do with the continuous take, it quickly wears off and becomes a gimmick, and then starts actively drawing attention to itself, almost like it's to distract from how thin the story actually is and how lacking it is in substance. I cannot name one notable thing that happened in the first hour - actually, in the entire movie - anything that makes me want to rewatch it. Put aside the continuous shot gimmick and there's just not much left to the movie itself. Even the climatic run during the attack, and the ending itself were both really underwhelming. The dialogue was dull, the emotional moments were predictable and manipulative, the bad guys were just cartoonishly evil obstacles, the sound design was drowned out by the score, I eventually couldn't wait for the whole thing to end. It felt like the movie has no substance beyond its continuous shot style. Overall, it was really underwhelming.

texto: I think this is so trite and overdrawn that it took me three attempts to finish through. Beyond the technical achievements of the film, much of the experience is bogged down by pacing issues and shallow dramaturgy, thoroughly reliant on a flimsy emotional stake that simply never stuck deep enough to elevate the otherwise amazing set pieces. Formally, too, there's almost no reason to invest any interest, as it never really moves past the gimmick of a oner, nor does it have the balls to fully commit to the bit. The camera wanders around and swings past our characters, but it feels more like a cam op hitting their marks rather than a fleshed out visual direction; it simply stages the next set-piece for us to see. The only time that the camera does feel like an actual cinematic instrument was in the trenches, where the claustrophobic corridors and shifting uniformed bodies serve to juxtapose the movements our characters are making; opposite against the huddled safety of the masses, away from the high walls of the trenches, into the open air of death. I should watch Dunkirk again.

texto: I saw this film on its first release in 2020 and I see from my history gave it 2.5 stars (indifferent/ mediocre). It’s one of the films where I find myself quite a bit out of step with the Letterboxd consensus, so I eventually got round to a re-watch to find out what I was missing. I have decided to revisit my mark - by knocking 1/2 mark off (2 stars = bad but not awful, so it has a redeeming feature). Given that there are many others who love this movie (and I appreciate that some of those have actually war experience and so cannot be dismissed), let me try to explain. Technically, this film is outstanding. The cinematography by the great Roger Deakins, the editing by Lee Smith, the lighting and the sound design - all beyond reproach. They all contribute to the apparent single shot presentation which is, at least as a technical achievement, rightly much lauded. At least in the first act and toward the end of the third this presentation drew me in and made the film seem immersive. But for me that is where it ends. This is a film that almost screams “Look how brilliant the director/ cinematographer/ sound is” in every moment at the cost of everything else. The plot is thin, contains far too many unlikely coincidences and events requiring a total suspension of belief. In particular there is a scene with a French woman and child that is tacky and adds nothing to the plot or action. The plot also drags a bit in places and it really needed to be faster paced. There are some fine cameos, particularly by Andrew Scott, Mark Strong and Benedict Cumberbatch, but the leads are ill-served by the script. This is a world populated by stereotypes - the Germans are all (very) bad,  the serving man the suffering salt of the earth. Beyond that there is no characterisation to speak of, and the lead character(s) are uncharismatic and totally emotionless. By the end of the film, I didn’t care what happened to anyone. There are of course other one shot presentation films - Birdman and Rope spring to mind - but none on the scale of this. For that reason, I suspect that 1917 might be on the syllabus of film courses for years to come. If I had been marking this film solely on technical achievement, certainly a 4.5, possibly a 5. But for the casual viewer, this is basically a gimmick film that is all about spectacle and special effects - more of an experience than a narrative film and you may find your attention wandering long before the end. While I admire the craft, I cannot recommend it to other than film students.

texto: Breathtaking, stunning, immersive cinematic masterpiece that showcases the horrors of World War I into a ticking clock survival thriller. Director Sam Mendes successfully strips away the typical political grandiosity of historical war epics to focus on a intimate, terrifyingly immediate human story of loyalty and perseverance. The film’s best element is that it is crafted to appear as one continuous, unbroken tracking shot unfolding in real time. Legendary cinematographer Roger Deakins uses clever camera movements, hidden cuts, and brilliant staging to pull the audience into the trenches alongside the soldiers. It removes the detachment of traditional editing, making you feel less like a viewer and more like a third runner on the mission. Early in the film, Blake points out chopped down cherry trees, noting that the scattered seeds will still grow back. Later, when Schofield is floating down a river choked with dead bodies, white cherry blossoms gently fall from the sky. It symbolizes that life and beauty will eventually outlast the cruelty of war. The ending beautifully captures that while the physical war continues unabated, Schofield has undergone a profound internal shift. Through Blake’s sacrifice, he moves from being a numb, detached survivor to a man who fully understands the value of human dignity and emotional connection. George MacKay and Dean Charles Chapman carries the film entirely on their shoulders. As the camera rarely leaves them, their performances required immense physical and emotional endurance. Both delivered a remarkably grounded and physical performance. With a script that intentionally lacks heavy dialogue or prolonged exposition dumps, MacKay and Chapman had to communicate raw vulnerability, fear, and sheer adrenaline through their facial expressions and body language. MacKay in particular, received significant praise for carrying the emotional weight of the film's second half. His ability to portray a quiet, desperate resilience that keeps the audience invested in the human drama amidst the chaotic spectacle of war. Overall 1917 is a breathtaking achievement that demands the biggest screen possible. Even if the narrative path is straightforward, the sheer scale of craftsmanship makes it an unforgettable, heart pounding journey.

texto: For *1917*, I think the obvious thing that fits your taste is the **cinematography and the illusion that you're following them in one continuous shot**. But I would not make it purely technical because the friendship and urgency of the mission are what give that filmmaking weight. 1917 is one of those films where the way it was made is almost as impressive as the story itself. The decision to make the film appear as one continuous shot is incredible. Rather than watching the war from a distance, the camera follows Blake and Schofield through everything. Across trenches, through fields, into abandoned buildings and eventually straight into battle. There’s rarely an opportunity to escape from what they’re experiencing, and that makes the whole mission feel much more intense. Roger Deakins’ cinematography is absolutely stunning. There are so many shots where I find myself thinking about how they actually managed to capture them, especially knowing how precisely the actors, camera crew, sets and effects had to work together to maintain the illusion of one continuous journey. The nighttime sequence through Écoust with the flares lighting the ruins is probably one of the best-looking sequences in the entire film. What really makes it work though is that all of that technical brilliance actually serves the story. The mission itself is incredibly simple: cross enemy territory and deliver a message that could save 1,600 men. Because you stay with Blake and Schofield for almost every step, you start feeling the distance, exhaustion and constant danger alongside them. The friendship between them gives it the emotional weight it needs too. What begins as two soldiers carrying out an order gradually becomes something much more personal, and there are moments that hit incredibly hard without the film needing to overdo them. I also love how the war is portrayed. It isn’t constantly trying to give you huge battles. Some of the most tense moments come from silence, empty trenches or simply not knowing what might be around the next corner. Then when the film does open up into something bigger, it feels enormous. And that final run across the battlefield while everyone else charges in the opposite direction is one of those scenes I could watch again and again. Brilliant cinematography, incredible attention to detail and a simple story made unbelievably intense by how it was filmed. Definitely one that made me appreciate just how much work can go into getting a shot exactly right.

texto: Breathtaking, stunning, immersive cinematic masterpiece that showcases the horrors of World War I into a ticking clock survival thriller. Director Sam Mendes successfully strips away the typical political grandiosity of historical war epics to focus on a intimate, terrifyingly immediate human story of loyalty and perseverance. The film’s best element is that it is crafted to appear as one continuous, unbroken tracking shot unfolding in real time. Legendary cinematographer Roger Deakins uses clever camera movements, hidden cuts, and brilliant staging to pull the audience into the trenches alongside the soldiers. It removes the detachment of traditional editing, making you feel less like a viewer and more like a third runner on the mission. Early in the film, Blake points out chopped down cherry trees, noting that the scattered seeds will still grow back. Later, when Schofield is floating down a river choked with dead bodies, white cherry blossoms gently fall from the sky. It symbolizes that life and beauty will eventually outlast the cruelty of war. The ending beautifully captures that while the physical war continues unabated, Schofield has undergone a profound internal shift. Through Blake’s sacrifice, he moves from being a numb, detached survivor to a man who fully understands the value of human dignity and emotional connection. George MacKay and Dean Charles Chapman carries the film entirely on their shoulders. As the camera rarely leaves them, their performances required immense physical and emotional endurance. Both delivered a remarkably grounded and physical performance. With a script that intentionally lacks heavy dialogue or prolonged exposition dumps, MacKay and Chapman had to communicate raw vulnerability, fear, and sheer adrenaline through their facial expressions and body language. MacKay in particular, received significant praise for carrying the emotional weight of the film's second half. His ability to portray a quiet, desperate resilience that keeps the audience invested in the human drama amidst the chaotic spectacle of war. Overall 1917 is a breathtaking achievement that demands the biggest screen possible. Even if the narrative path is straightforward, the sheer scale of craftsmanship makes it an unforgettable, heart pounding journey.

texto: For *1917*, I think the obvious thing that fits your taste is the **cinematography and the illusion that you're following them in one continuous shot**. But I would not make it purely technical because the friendship and urgency of the mission are what give that filmmaking weight. 1917 is one of those films where the way it was made is almost as impressive as the story itself. The decision to make the film appear as one continuous shot is incredible. Rather than watching the war from a distance, the camera follows Blake and Schofield through everything. Across trenches, through fields, into abandoned buildings and eventually straight into battle. There’s rarely an opportunity to escape from what they’re experiencing, and that makes the whole mission feel much more intense. Roger Deakins’ cinematography is absolutely stunning. There are so many shots where I find myself thinking about how they actually managed to capture them, especially knowing how precisely the actors, camera crew, sets and effects had to work together to maintain the illusion of one continuous journey. The nighttime sequence through Écoust with the flares lighting the ruins is probably one of the best-looking sequences in the entire film. What really makes it work though is that all of that technical brilliance actually serves the story. The mission itself is incredibly simple: cross enemy territory and deliver a message that could save 1,600 men. Because you stay with Blake and Schofield for almost every step, you start feeling the distance, exhaustion and constant danger alongside them. The friendship between them gives it the emotional weight it needs too. What begins as two soldiers carrying out an order gradually becomes something much more personal, and there are moments that hit incredibly hard without the film needing to overdo them. I also love how the war is portrayed. It isn’t constantly trying to give you huge battles. Some of the most tense moments come from silence, empty trenches or simply not knowing what might be around the next corner. Then when the film does open up into something bigger, it feels enormous. And that final run across the battlefield while everyone else charges in the opposite direction is one of those scenes I could watch again and again. Brilliant cinematography, incredible attention to detail and a simple story made unbelievably intense by how it was filmed. Definitely one that made me appreciate just how much work can go into getting a shot exactly right.

texto: Leider nicht direkt meines. Die "Dollars"-Trilogie steht schon seit Anbeginn der Zeit auf meiner Watchlist und irgendwie habe ich mich immer etwas davor gesträubt. Vermutlich aufgrund der Tatsache, dass das alles Western sind. Denn mit diesem Genre konnte ich noch nie viel anfangen, hatte allerdings auch die Hoffnung, von eines Besseren belehrt zu werden. Leider war das nicht direkt der Fall. Was ich aber sagen muss ist, dass "A Fistful of Dollars" Momente hatte. Es gab hier und da Szenen, die selbst mich gepackt haben, die actionreich und einfach spaßig waren. Das Problem war vermutlich nur, dass ich nicht vollkommen in der Richtigen Stimmung war. Ich habe mir allerdings ein Szenario ausgemalt, in dem diese Filme besser funktionieren können und ich werde es definitiv erneut probieren, wenn dies der Fall ist. Besonders eben, da ich gesehen habe, dass der Film Momente hat, die eben nicht vollkommen funktioniert haben, auch wenn ich mir das gewünscht hätte. Was aber definitiv sehr stark war, war der Score, der für mich fast den ganzen Film getragen hat. Was Ennio Morricone hier abgeliefert hat, war großartig und hat den Film für mich definitiv aufgewertet. Das Problem ist nur, dass ich die Handlung abgesehen davon leider extrem langweilig fand. Ich kann selbst nicht sagen, woran genau das lag, aber irgendwie kam es mir so vor, als würde nichts passieren. Wie gesagt: hier und da gab es Momente, aber diese waren mir dann doch nicht auf dem Niveau, dass sie noch wirklich viel retten konnte. Sie haben den Film noch okay gemacht, aber für mehr hat es leider nicht gereicht. 2,5/5 Sternen.

texto: J’ai bien été diverti! La musique est extraordinaire vraiment Enio jtm et le film est très bien rythmé. Problème qui m’empêche de mettre une meilleure note, je sais pas pq mon cerveau n’arrivait PAS à ce concentrer tout le long du film. J’ai compris les enjeux principaux avec notre Clint Eastwood qui intervient dans un conflit entre deux clans qui se battent pour…… jle dirai pas 😜, mais vraiment mon cerveau était éteint pendant 1h30 et j’arrivais pas à suivre le cours des événements (ça ne m’a pas empêché de passer un agréable moment nevertheless!). La fin est super tuff et la mentalité de Joe vis à vis de l’Etat en opposition à celle qu’il a envers les gangs est cool. Aussi, je sais pas c’est quoi le problème de France TV mais WHAT THE FUCK les sous titres français genre, à de nombreuses reprises les sous titres ont rien à voir avec les dialogues et des fois y’en a qui apparaissent de nul part ; c’est sûrement basé sur la VF de l’époque mais j’ai eu la flemme de vérifier. En tout cas jvais m’empresser d’aller mater Yojimbo histoire de voir l’original et d’aller avec la rétrospective Kurosawa en salle actuellement, et j’ai hâte d’enchaîner avec la suite de la trilogie 🤠

He walked with this film, so the third one could run. That being said, the whole climax of this film is badass.

texto: This movie blows. It blows hard and long. The opening twenty minutes were pretty good. No characters were deeply written, made stupid decisions, there was bad dialogue, and there was overall bad acting. texto: At this point, I can confidently say that old westerns are my least favorite genre. The acting is never up to par for me and that holds true here, as well. Clint Eastwood is passable as the lead, but he feels too flat a lot of the time. There's no range or charisma. I recognize that that is part of the character he's playing, but I think he takes it too far. It's hard to tell if the supporting actors are awful or if it's just the TERRIBLE dubbing, which distracted me the entire movie. Dubbing seems nearly impossible to do well, or at the least, back in the Old Hollywood days. Every dubbed performance here feels so stiff. The energy never truly matches the scene itself. I don't really care that the mouths don't match the words perfectly, just that the performance doesn't match the physicality of what the actors are doing. On the positive side, the pacing and editing in this film are easily better than most other westerns I've seen, which all seem to drag out the runtime needlessly. This movie is 99 minutes long and there's zero extra fluff from what I can tell. The plot is interesting, even if its execution comes across as cheesy at times due to the writing and dubbed performances. The third act is surprisingly cool. I went in with tempered expectations and they were basically met. I'll stick around for the rest of the trilogy since The Good, The Bad, and The Ugly has such a great reputation, but I won't hold my breath. Old westerns just aren't my thing. 56/100

texto: Went into A Fistful of Dollars expecting a tense western showdown and instead got 100 straight minutes of Clint Eastwood squinting at people like he’s trying to remember where he parked his horse. The pacing moves with all the urgency of a tumbleweed filing tax returns. Entire scenes consist of men silently staring at each other while a harmonica wheezes somewhere in the distance. By the time somebody finally got shot, I’d emotionally aged into a frontier grandparent. The storyline is somehow both incredibly simple and completely confusing. Two families hate each other, Clint wanders between them doing… something? Half the movie feels like arriving late to a barbecue where everyone already knows the gossip except you. Characters appear, glare ominously, then vanish forever like NPCs with unfinished dialogue trees. And emotional complexity? The deepest character development is “this guy looks sweaty and angry now.” Clint Eastwood’s character has roughly the emotional range of a granite countertop wearing a poncho. I’ve had more psychologically layered interactions with self checkout machines. Still, the soundtrack slaps. So congratulations to the trumpet guy for carrying the entire film on his back like a weary mule.

texto: The genre that Leone is really known for and made him famous worldwide - Spaghetti Westerns! Personally I am not the biggest fan of Westerns in general, haven’t seen many of them and never been that keen to watch them either. But when people talk about Westerns there are few names there ARE this genre, one of those being Leone himself and the great Clint Eastwood, who acted in them and has made a quite few himself, even won a few Oscars. Let’s just say the first freaking second already started with a bang - a wonderful soundtrack by the great Ennio Morricone! The plot is straight to the point and our antihero is a great man. The supporting cast is so-so, besides Silvanito and Piripero. The scenery of Spain in the background is breathtaking and set design is TOP! I love that it is 1h and 30min long, the perfect length. BUT and there is a HUGE but here - Sergio Leone is a THIEF, who stole the film plot-by-plot from the great himself - Akira Kurosawa’s ’Yojimbo’ and that fact pisses me off! I haven’t seen the film, but now I am contemplating if I should watch that next or watch the two other films before I watch it and I INTED TO WATCH IT, because I have to see it quickly.

tema: Trilha sonora e música de Ennio Morricone
exemplo: A música de Ennio Morricone é mencionada como um dos pontos altos do filme, com destaque para a trilha sonora marcante e a composição que se tornou icônica para o gênero.
texto: The problem with this film will always be that Yojimbo is obviously better (and somehow, despite being longer, a great deal more urgently-paced), but despite its extraordinarily close resemblance to its model, this is happily much less redundant than one could easily fear. For one thing, Clint Eastwood's vibe is completely different than Mifune Toshirō's, not in a way that I'm prepared to call either one "better", but it does mean that there's a sneering nihilistic bitterness to Leone's vision of pointless cycles of violence that Kurosawa's more sardonic but also more human vision doesn't quite aim for. For another thing, color really changes this: Leone didn't invent the Italian-production-shot-in-Spain Western, but he pushed it to astonishing new heights, the hot yellow of the dead earth creating a feeling of dusty exhaustion beneath the taunting coolness of the blue sky that makes the films feel set in a mythic neverwhen of endless desert studded with barely-extant towns (which is, for that matter, another very consequential difference: Kurosawa's film takes place in a historicized Japan, but Leone's takes place in a hazy, hellish fantasy of The American Wild West, and it just feels dreamier). This was my first chance to watch the entirety of the Arrow restoration from 2025, and it's a real "scales fall from my eyes" moment - just jaw-dropping how overwhelming the earth tones are when they've been calibrated and shaded properly. Would absolutely be a classic even if Leone hadn't ever stepped foot on a film set again, but in context, one can't help but note that this is a very exploratory first effort: the aggressive close-ups slashed together in brutal jab-jab-jab edits are a remarkable gesture (and one that isn't in any way indebted to Yojimbo ), but you can tell he hasn't figured out how to balance them yet, either as compositions or within the edit; they're very assertive but they don't have the weight that they'll have in the two follow-ups. Still, I think is to be celebrated for creating a template that could be built upon to such magnificent effect rather than condemned for not immediately representing the high-water-mark of its genre. Also, Ennio Morricone's work here is totally awe-inspiring , lonely windy whistling, raspy male vocalizations, and menacing Mexican & Texan instrumentation combining to create a sonic concept for "The West" that as far as I know was invented in this movie and has, to me at least, absolutely defined the way I think about how that time and place sound. And amazingly, this is another respect in which both sequels clearly improve on it! ( Previously reviewed at Alternate Ending )

texto: Reel Review: A Fistful of Dollars is a stellar remake. It is a rock ‘n’ roll western about an anti-hero out to make money by pitting two rival gang against each other. Leone expertly crafts a tense film with a cynical and deadly attitude. It’s the perfect flick for the transformative 1960s era which builds on the myth of the American western from the perspective of Italian and Spanish filmmakers. Few films have had such impact from its iconic score to the stoic lead character. The movie’s working title was “The Magnificent Stranger” and Eastwood effortlessly plays that wandering loner. He’s cool, clever, confident, charismatic, and cold blooded. The role shot him to superstardom and I can’t imagine anyone else playing him. The entire cast is made up of some solid actors from all over the map. The script is extremely similar to Yojimbo, yet with a setting and style all its own. The extreme closeups are one of the aspects that make this movie stand out along with the brutal action scenes. Morricone’s score is also an element that is absolutely recognizable. The movie brings a gritty and dirty look to the old west due to excellent sets, locations, costumes, hair, and makeup. Boredom never sets in thanks to good editing, bursts of violence, and a perfect mix of humor and tension. This is a groundbreaking movie and it remains an enjoyable watch. The Man With No Name trilogy Blu-ray set is good. There are a few issues with the video and audio, but it is a solid presentation overall. A few bonus features are included. The best element is the commentary which bring out so much detail into the story of the making of the film as well as the film itself and it’s historical impact. It may be worth finding a 4K edition, but make sure it includes this commentary. Reel Themes: Greed, revenge, justice Reel Recommendations: My Darling Clementine High Noon Hondo Shane The Fastest Gun Alive Ride Lonesome Yojimbo Sanjuro Reel Worldview: Psalm 10:3 For the wicked boasts of the desires of his soul, and the one greedy for gain curses and renounces the LORD.

Instead, Smith brought his own 90s Fresh Prince charisma, hip-hop energy, and charm, making Genie his own. The production design is colorful, festive, and theatrical. The grand parade sequence for "Friend Like Me" and "Prince Ali" is pure Bollywood-inspired spectacle that translates surprisingly well to live-action. Marwan Kenzari’s Jafar is unfortunately pretty forgettable. Instead of the sinister, imposing villain from the animated classic, he comes across as a bit too young and mild-mannered

texto: Aladdin  is one of those movies that just sticks with you because it’s wild, loud, and honestly pretty funny. The Genie is all over the place, He’s easily one of the funniest parts of the movie. But when you actually pay attention to the story, there’s something kind of weird going on with Princess Jasmine. She’s supposed to be this rebellious princess who wants to make her own choices, but she barely gets to control what happens in her own story. Jasmine talks a lot about wanting freedom and not wanting someone else to choose her future, but the movie doesn’t really give her much room to do anything about it. Her dad is trying to decide who she should marry, Jafar is constantly trying to control everything, and even Aladdin spends most of the movie lying to her. Jasmine tries to stand up for herself, but the story keeps moving around her. It’s like she’s talking, but nobody is really listening. Another thing I noticed is how much everyone in Agrabah is constantly talking, singing, arguing, or making deals. There’s always something happening. Meanwhile, Jasmine feels like she gets pushed into the background. She has important things to say, but the movie seems more interested in Aladdin, Genie, Jafar, and all the chaos happening around them. It almost feels like Jasmine is there, but her voice gets lost in all the noise. That’s also what makes the movie kind of absurd. The whole world is crazy with magic carpets, a talking parrot, a magical lamp, and a Genie who can basically do anything. The rules don’t always make much sense, but that’s part of what makes it fun. Everyone is chasing something, whether it’s power, freedom, love, or just getting what they want. Jasmine wants freedom, but she doesn’t really get to figure out what that means for herself. Overall, I still think Aladdin is a really fun movie. The animation is colorful, the music is memorable, and Genie brings so much energy to the movie. I just wish Jasmine had more control over her own story because she actually has the potential to be one of the strongest characters. Instead, she sometimes feels like she’s just reacting to whatever Aladdin, Jafar, or her dad does next.

texto: A retelling of the classic animated movie that has the spectacle but lacks the dazzling splendor that made the original film timeless.  This film adds a bit more depth to Agrabah as well as some exposition on Aladdin’s parents and Jasmine’s mother.  The acting was unfortunately the film’s weakest point and Will Smith is no Robin Williams but he does try to do something different.  Overall not a great live action adaptation but certainly not the worst.  Fun at times and the set pieces and wardrobe was beautiful, but this was no diamond in the rough.

texto: “He’s a little dim, but you’re just getting married. It’s not like you have to talk to him.” Guy Ritchie’s remake of the 1992 animated classic follows Aladdin as he discovers a magic lamp that contains a genie who helps him impress Princess Jasmine of Agrabah by disguising him as a prince, only to raise the suspicion of the evil vizier Jafar. Another unnecessary remake thats only success lies in the portrayal of the Genie that toed a line between a fresh take and homage, with Jasmine’s handmaiden Dalia - Genie’s future wife - a decent new character who didn’t detract from the story. Their chemistry surpassed Aladdin and Jasmine’s with much less time spent together throughout. At its worst when it’s copying the original as the flaws become glaring, especially in the portrayal of Jafar who was neither menacing nor effective as a conjurer even with the full power of the lamp. The songs were uninspiring and lacked any magic from “A Whole New World” to “Friend Like Me” to Jasmine’s new song “Speechless” that succeeds in showing off her voice while still being lacking. Cast includes Mena Massoud, Naomi Scott, Will Smith, Marwan Kenzari, Navid Negahban, Nasim Pedrad, Billy Magnussen, and Alan Tudyk as Iago, with Frank Welker the lone returnee voicing Abu.

Will Smith was so much fun as the Genie. He definitely brings his own personality to the character rather than trying to copy Robin Williams, and I actually enjoyed his version. The movie is entertaining and the musical numbers are really enjoyable. I especially liked seeing the original story brought to life in a more modern way. It’s definitely not as magical as the original, which will always be hard to beat, but I still really enjoyed watching it. A fun and colorful remake that I’d happily watch again.

texto: It was always a tall order for Will Smith to step into Robin Williams’ iconic role. But if you give him the grace of imagining casting another big personality (albeit from music as opposed to comedy) Smith is a strong choice and he DOES A GOOD JOB. The real problem is Guy Ritchie having not one iota of interest or imagination to do anything but phone in his version of this story. The “One Jump” and “Prince Ali” sequences betray an utter lack of creativity on Ritchie’s part. A shame because other aspects of this film are strong enough to have made an impact in another life.

texto: I honestly fell asleep the first watch through, so I had to watch it again. This is my first time watching either Aladdin, so I don't feel disturbed as others might feel about all the additions, replacements, and whatever. I felt like this version did a better—but not good—job of respecting the culture in the Middle East. The women aren't as hypersexualized in this version as it was in the original animation, straying away from Orientalism just a bit. In fact, everyone is a lot more clothed than shown in the animation. However, I'm no expert, but I've noticed that rather than representing the Middle East, there were many Indian elements like the clothes in the movie. I'm glad they didn't make Jasmine look like the typical belly dancer stereotype, but they still failed to depict what Arabian women would actually wear. Moreover, Jasmine was able to jump with the pole in the original as she was running away with Aladdin, which showed some of her fearlessness (that ultimately never got fleshed out), but in this one, she chickens out. That pissed me off because if they're trying to empower Jasmine, there was no reason to make her back out in this scene. Also, there was no need to leave her frozen in place at such a critical moment, where she could've proven herself. Sadly, the men have to save this damsel in distress once more. What surprised me the most was The Sultan having more aura in this movie. In the original, this guy was just an idiot with almost no thought of his own, but in this one, he tried to stand his ground. I guess they donated some of Jasmine's fearlessness to a man who doesn't even have a name. I really don't care if they bring some random handmaiden into the movie, but if they can make changes like that, I would've loved if they removed more of the harmful stereotypes and made Jasmine independent. It honestly feels like they watered down the original to make it seem less problematic when, really, the true meaning and intent are still there. There are several Israel sympathizers in the cast as well that have also played violent roles in other media. Yes, there's a more diverse cast that come from the Middle East but at what cost? The soundtrack did have bangers, but it sounded more Western than Middle Eastern. For example, when Jasmine played that one instrument, it just sounded like a regular guitar you'd hear in the US. When you look at the composers behind these songs, you'll quickly notice that none of them are Arab; it all adds up. As I talked about earlier with things being watered down, the lyrics to "Arabian Nights" were tweaked to make the people seem less barbaric in Arabia, but they still call them barbaric. Overall, the movie definitely made some nice changes from the original, but they weren't done right. This could've been so much better.

texto: A live action that comes off more like a Broadway show that ended up in the wrong place. And that pretty much explains everything that doesn't work. There's a whole musical number shoved into the middle of the film that plays out like a Disney park parade, way more than anything that matters to the story. The CGI is overdone and bad. The problem isn't the target audience, a teen adventure in the same lane as Descendants and Zombies . It's the quality of the production as a whole, even with the effort of putting a superstar like Will Smith in the cast. There are a few isolated stretches of decent rom com, but nothing you haven't seen before. Another thing that stands out, compared to the original cartoon, is how much time Will Smith spends as a human and builds a relationship with Dalia, Jasmine's handmaiden. That's not in the original at all. And what's holding up what little quality is left is the soundtrack, excellent as always in Disney films, which only proves the point: when the music is the only standout in a movie, maybe it should've just stayed on a stage.

texto: Franchement, j’ai bien aimé ce Aladdin. Comme pour les autres live-action Disney, le film ne reprend pas exactement le dessin animé original et se permet quelques changements, mais personnellement ça ne m’a pas dérangé. J’ai particulièrement apprécié les chansons, qui fonctionnent vraiment bien et donnent beaucoup d’énergie au film. Et gros coup de cœur pour le Génie de Will Smith. J’avais un peu peur de la comparaison avec Robin Williams, mais finalement il apporte sa propre personnalité au personnage. Je l’ai trouvé vraiment drôle et très agréable à suivre. Dans l’ensemble, c’est un bon divertissement, coloré, musical et plutôt fun. Ce n’est peut-être pas le meilleur live-action Disney que j’ai vu, mais j’ai passé un très bon moment devant.

tema: Crítica à propaganda e ao patriotismo
exemplo: Reviews medianas apontam que o filme parece glorificar a guerra e o patriotismo americano, funcionando como propaganda que alimenta o poder de soft do país. Reviews consideram a abordagem simplista e que o filme não critica as ações militares de forma abrangente.
texto: 'MERICA FUCK YEAH American Sniper is probably the most patriotic movie I've ever watched. It doesn't try to hide this fact, constantly pushing the flag loving American way in the viewers face throughout. This movie very much feels like an American propaganda piece. And despite that, for the most part, its a fun action movie. My issues lie with the fact it isn't just that. Chris Kyle's story in this movie is paced pretty poorly. It's not really believable, overly dramatic and romanticised. The movie excels when it focuses less on the American and more on the Sniper. There's just this random shift in the story to try to create compassion for Chris Kyle that just doesn't work, it's too forced and unbelievable. Now the sniping is fun! The action is exciting. The meat of the movie is there. I wish there was a little more focus on the Sniping itself it feels like it was more a vehicle to tell the story through. But there were a few stand out moments. A simple American Propaganda piece. Watch it with that in mind, it can be a good time!

tema: Crítica à propaganda e ao patriotismo
exemplo: Reviews medianas apontam que o filme parece glorificar a guerra e o patriotismo americano, funcionando como propaganda que alimenta o poder de soft do país. Reviews consideram a abordagem simplista e que o filme não critica as ações militares de forma abrangente.
texto: Once again Clint Eastwood doesn’t simply create a conservative-wet-dream here, even if sometimes in the discourse about this film, the idea might come up; I definitely disagree with the claim, that this is a glorification of the Iraq-war or any US-military operation in the western Asian area of the past 30 years. I think Eastwood simply tells the story of war from the perspective of a “brain-washed” American soldier and thus wants to us see, what someone sees, who was brought up with a rifle in their hands already and frightened by the media, who created the picture of the “dangerous Muslim terrorist” in the minds of Americans after 9/11. The central question to ask is: does Eastwood side with Bradley Cooper’s character or does he just observe his actions. When you think, that he sides with “Chris Kyle”, then this film is on the same territory as something like Michael Bay’s “Pearl Harbour”, where the US-Army is glorified. I don’t think that we are on such territory here. Through the direction and also through Cooper’s performance there is always a distinct rift between the viewer and “Kyle” as a character. Eastwood doesn’t allow us to fully identify with him. He is definitely depicted as a slightly weird guy, who is drawn into the entire topic of war and the horrors, that come with it and who also doesn’t really understand, what his actions really mean; he is someone, who cannot see clear about the horrors, that he commits, which is also why he doesn’t feel sorry. But that doesn’t mean that Eastwood himself wants us to be the same. For me this is — much like other Clint Eastwood movies, whose style of conservative filmmaking is (as I have pointed out recently in my review for “J. Edgar”) much more nuanced — an observers view on a system, where technically we should feel pity for those people, who are unable to see behind the curtain and fall right into the traps. Thus it’s also a bit dull to call this movie out for being too focussed on the American perspective and seemingly uninterested about the casualties that this man creates in Iraq. texto: This movie has an interesting point to make about how difficult it is for soldiers to readjust to normal life after the trauma of war. Unfortunately, that idea never feels fully explored. The perspective on the war is extremely one sided, there are too few moments that really show his struggle outside the battlefield, and the whole thing often feels closer to military glorification than to a deeper reflection on what war takes from a person. Because of that, what could have been a great film ends up feeling just average. PS: The fake baby still haunts me.

texto: Testosterona, patriotismo, explosiones, Texas, AMÉRICA🦅🦅 Bueno no es tan descarado como en alguna otra película pero se nota claramente la americanada, a pesar de ser una biografía de Chris Kyle, uno de los mejores francotiradores de la historia. A pesar de la simpleza que estas películas suelen tener, aquí se da mucho enfoque a los efectos que los veteranos experimentan tras volver a casa del campo de batalla. Chris está físicamente en Texas, sin embargo, su mente sigue oyendo tiros y helicópteros como cuando estaba en Iraq. Para él, la guerra al principio tuvo un carácter colectivo, se alistó para “defender a su país” y utilizar sus habilidades para proteger al resto de soldados compatriotas; sin embargo, a medida que la película avanza, su misión va adquiriendo un carácter más personal, incluso poniendo en riesgo la vida de sus camaradas y la suya, con el fin de abatir al francotirador enemigo. El hecho de que sea una biografía real es algo interesante, pero a la vez te hace replantearte varias cosas. Las atrocidades que se cometieron en esa guerra (y las que no se muestran) y los efectos que tanto la población civil como los soldados destinados están por sufrir es la mejor propaganda antibelicista del mundo. Al final, la guerra es desmontada por la verdad. Lo que debería haber sido la biografía de un hombre (aunque respetable en muchos aspectos) que ama la guerra, se ha convertido en propaganda en contra de aquello a lo que amaba, algo irónico, ¿no? En conclusión, peli entretenida si tienes un viaje de poco más de dos horas y no has dormido las suficientes horas como para reflexionar bien sobre una película.

Because of that, what could have been a great film ends up feeling just average. PS: The fake baby still haunts me.

texto: Once again Clint Eastwood doesn’t simply create a conservative-wet-dream here, even if sometimes in the discourse about this film, the idea might come up; I definitely disagree with the claim, that this is a glorification of the Iraq-war or any US-military operation in the western Asian area of the past 30 years. I think Eastwood simply tells the story of war from the perspective of a “brain-washed” American soldier and thus wants to us see, what someone sees, who was brought up with a rifle in their hands already and frightened by the media, who created the picture of the “dangerous Muslim terrorist” in the minds of Americans after 9/11. The central question to ask is: does Eastwood side with Bradley Cooper’s character or does he just observe his actions. When you think, that he sides with “Chris Kyle”, then this film is on the same territory as something like Michael Bay’s “Pearl Harbour”, where the US-Army is glorified. I don’t think that we are on such territory here. Through the direction and also through Cooper’s performance there is always a distinct rift between the viewer and “Kyle” as a character. Eastwood doesn’t allow us to fully identify with him. He is definitely depicted as a slightly weird guy, who is drawn into the entire topic of war and the horrors, that come with it and who also doesn’t really understand, what his actions really mean; he is someone, who cannot see clear about the horrors, that he commits, which is also why he doesn’t feel sorry. But that doesn’t mean that Eastwood himself wants us to be the same. For me this is — much like other Clint Eastwood movies, whose style of conservative filmmaking is (as I have pointed out recently in my review for “J. Edgar”) much more nuanced — an observers view on a system, where technically we should feel pity for those people, who are unable to see behind the curtain and fall right into the traps. Thus it’s also a bit dull to call this movie out for being too focussed on the American perspective and seemingly uninterested about the casualties that this man creates in Iraq. Eastwood simply doesn’t want to show this here; his focus is the story of a soldier’s life, that is destroyed by a war-machinery, that makes him believe to be heroic part of something, while eventually he’s just ammunition for the interest of someone else — kind of the idea that the first two acts of “Born of the Fourth of July” follows. This is also hauntingly shown, when “Kyle” is back home for a short time and shows his son to use a rifle, just like his father did. The cycle of violence won’t stop here, because these people are trapped in the world of serving someone else’s interests — something that’s incredibly far away from the ideology that I’d associate with Clint Eastwood. So all in all it’s a film about the lost lives of soldiers and as such it succeeds mostly. I decided to still give a rather mid rating, because for me the runtime is too long, especially since the story gets a little repetitive the longer “Kyle” stays in the war-zone. A higher focus on “Kyle’s” family life and the destruction of it would have made a better movie in my opinion, even if Eastwood is able to create some intense fighting scenes. But this should have been more like “The Best Years of our Lives” or “Apocalypse Now” and less like “Warfare”, because there’s no way that I won’t get bored at 130 minutes of people shooting around in the desert.

It also felt off seeing Chris and others willingness to fight and die in a war that we now know was pretty much unjustified; by the time this movie had come out, it was already well established that Iraq didn’t have any WMDs, and that the US had invaded the area based off of blind fear and false reports. I wish the movie was more nuanced and delved more into this towards the end to contrast the earlier excitement of the soldiers instead of being all “AMERICA FUCK YEAH” the whole time

Great if you love cinematic propaganda and very expensive sound effects; less great if you were hoping for a fourth facial expression.

texto: ​"Aim small, miss small." ​It is incredibly easy to see why this gets written off as the ultimate "dude-bro American propaganda" movie. It is intensely, unapologetically American, and it absolutely flattens a complex geopolitical conflict into a straightforward "America is the hero" narrative. You could go on for hours about this, and honestly, most of those critiques would be entirely well-placed. It’s also not a technically brilliant film—the pacing can feel incredibly choppy, the visual style is pretty flat, and yes, that notorious fake plastic baby completely pulls you out of the moment ​But if you dismiss it solely based on that surface-level wrapping, you're missing the forest for the trees. Despite those filmmaking flaws and the questionable depiction of America's role in the Iraq War, the movie still works because it succeeds entirely at what it actually set out to do: deliver a narrow, personal character study. ​At its core, this is about the psychological toll of deployment ​American Sniper isn't trying to be a sprawling macro-commentary on the ethics of the Iraq War. It’s about what happens to a human being when their entire reality shrinks down to the crosshairs of a sniper's scope. Clint Eastwood does a good job showing how the cumulative effect of these tours slowly erodes a person's ability to exist in normal civilian life with the time constraints that come with creating a Hollywood blockbuster ​The combat sequences are tense, aided by some incredibly sharp audio design, but the real hitter is the silence once Chris Kyle gets back to Texas. Bradley Cooper sells that weight, showing us a man who is physically sitting on his couch with his family, but mentally still scanning rooftops thousands of miles away. ​It’s wrapped in patriotic bravado and hindered by some clunky filmmaking, but underneath it all is a genuinely interesting look at the personal cost of trauma and duty. ​If you judge it by its true intent, rather than its politics or its technical polish, it does hits the target. ​All that said, it would be incredibly biased to completely dismiss the aforementioned flaws. They absolutely impact the viewing experience, and the film does require you to actively overlook some of its shortcomings in order to see the forest through what are, admittedly, some rather large trees. But if you can manage that, its true intent still shines. 3.5/5

texto: ​"Aim small, miss small." ​It is incredibly easy to see why this gets written off as the ultimate "dude-bro American propaganda" movie. It is intensely, unapologetically American, and it absolutely flattens a complex geopolitical conflict into a straightforward "America is the hero" narrative. You could go on for hours about this, and honestly, most of those critiques would be entirely well-placed. It’s also not a technically brilliant film—the pacing can feel incredibly choppy, the visual style is pretty flat, and yes, that notorious fake plastic baby completely pulls you out of the moment ​But if you dismiss it solely based on that surface-level wrapping, you're missing the forest for the trees. Despite those filmmaking flaws and the questionable depiction of America's role in the Iraq War, the movie still works because it succeeds entirely at what it actually set out to do: deliver a narrow, personal character study. ​At its core, this is about the psychological toll of deployment ​American Sniper isn't trying to be a sprawling macro-commentary on the ethics of the Iraq War. It’s about what happens to a human being when their entire reality shrinks down to the crosshairs of a sniper's scope. Clint Eastwood does a good job showing how the cumulative effect of these tours slowly erodes a person's ability to exist in normal civilian life with the time constraints that come with creating a Hollywood blockbuster ​The combat sequences are tense, aided by some incredibly sharp audio design, but the real hitter is the silence once Chris Kyle gets back to Texas. Bradley Cooper sells that weight, showing us a man who is physically sitting on his couch with his family, but mentally still scanning rooftops thousands of miles away. ​It’s wrapped in patriotic bravado and hindered by some clunky filmmaking, but underneath it all is a genuinely interesting look at the personal cost of trauma and duty. ​If you judge it by its true intent, rather than its politics or its technical polish, it does hits the target. ​All that said, it would be incredibly biased to completely dismiss the aforementioned flaws. They absolutely impact the viewing experience, and the film does require you to actively overlook some of its shortcomings in order to see the forest through what are, admittedly, some rather large trees. But if you can manage that, its true intent still shines. 3.5/5

texto: American Sniper works because it makes the story feel personal. The film is tense, well staged, and easy to become emotionally invested in. You are not just watching military operations from a distance. You are watching what those experiences do to the person living through them. That is what makes the film compelling. The action sequences are intense, but the quieter moments matter just as much because they show the psychological weight that comes with everything happening on screen. There is a constant feeling that the character is caught between two worlds. The battlefield. And home. And the transition between them never feels simple. That makes the story easy to connect with on an emotional level, even if the actual experiences are obviously far removed from everyday life. The direction does a good job of making the tension immediate. You understand the pressure of making decisions in seconds. You feel how quickly situations can change. And you understand why those experiences do not simply disappear when someone returns home. That emotional side is what stayed with me most. The film is not perfect, but it is gripping, well performed, and strong enough to make you care about the person at the center of it. A tense and emotionally engaging war drama that works best when it focuses on the psychological weight carried home from the battlefield.

texto: I found myself bothered by numerous “plot holes” and issues with the story during this, only to look it up and find out that some of the most ridiculous shit in this movie is actually real. Yes it is based on “some fo real shit” as stated in the opening of the movie, but some of these details I just couldn’t believe. Yes, Ron Stallworth actually made the mistake of using his own name when first contacting the KKK. Yes, he actually got a white detective to handle in person interactions while he spoke to members on the phone. Yes, not a single KKK member noticed that their voices were different. Yes, when David Duke came to Colorado Springs, Stallworth’s police chief actually chose to assign him (the only black man in the entire force) to Duke’s protection, and when he objected his chief actually told him that “no one else is available”. All of this seemed pretty convenient while I was watching and I was ready to hate, but it turns out all of these details are true lol. Every scene with Laura Harrier in it, is trash af I’m sorry it just is. The chemistry btwn her and JDW is just completely nonexistent. All that being said this is good enough to watch for the one time and I was entertained but it didn’t do much else for me.

texto: Segunda película que veo de Spike Lee, segunda decepción que me llevo. Sinceramente no tengo demasiado que reprocharle, no me parece una mala película, puedo apreciar perfectamente lo que hace, pero al igual que me pasó con Inside Man, terminé la película pensando que me gustó más lo que Spike Lee quería decir, que la película que hizo para decirlo. BlacKkKlansman está cargadísima de problemáticas sociales y raciales, o sea, ésta directamente gira en torno a una historia real sobre la secta racista más conocida de la historia. Y claramente banco el mensaje, la crítica y lo absurdo que resulta todo esto. El tema es que la película nunca me llevó un punto más allá. La premisa es cuanto menos entretenida de ver, y tiene situaciones que en el papel deberían ser tensísimas o incómodas, pero en ningún momento percibí que la película llegara a explotar realmente. Todo avanzaba y rara vez sentía que algo tuviera verdadero peso, incluso la historia termina siendo bastante predecible. Y aunque no tengo ningún problema con los finales felices, este me pareció demasiado hollywoodense para tratarse de una historia basada en hechos reales. De hecho, el cierre terminó de confirmarme esa sensación, ya que en vez de sentir que la película había llegado naturalmente a un punto de quiebre, sentí que Spike necesitaba detenerse para recordarme cuál era el mensaje que acababa de ver durante dos horas. Tal vez también tengan algo que ver las expectativas. Ya que ésta, junto a Malcolm X y Do the Right Thing son películas que llevaba muchísimo tiempo queriendo ver, y entre las críticas y todo lo que se escucha sobre ellas, terminé llegando con las expectativas por las nubes. Esperaba que esto me demostrara por qué Spike Lee ES Spike Lee, pero no pasó. Aún con todo esto, le tengo una fe increíble a las otras dos.

texto: Je ne parviens pas à comprendre le concept de ce film qui est censé dénoncer le racisme, l’antisémitisme et l’homophobie aux Etats-Unis à travers l’histoire vraie d’un policier Noir qui est parvenu à infiltrer le Ku Klux Klan dans les années 70, mais dont la légèreté de ton, voire la nonchalance des personnages, contraste trop avec la gravité du sujet. Cette hésitation dans le traitement du film, entre images d’archives qui font froid dans le dos et scènes comiques à la sauce Starsky et Hutch, noie ainsi le propos dans un mélange des genres qui ne convainc pas. Si l’humour s’avère une arme cinématographique souvent efficace pour dénoncer des actes répréhensibles, il l’est bien plus quand l’intégralité du film repose sur la comédie. Ici, l'ensemble est trop caricatural et Spike Lee semble trop hésiter entre drame, pamphlet et scènes de pure comédie (pas toujours drôles, d’ailleurs), produisant une oscillation contre-productive qui dessert son sujet. Si le projet demeure louable, on est bien loin des fulgurances passées du réalisateur.

texto: What Spike Lee does is present this film as radical critique when it's actually functioning as counterinsurgence. On the surface you get a satisfying story where a Black cop infiltrates and disrupts the Klan. But that completely obscures the actual history that white supremacy wasn't ann external enemy. It was built into law enforcement and governance itself. The real problem is, it's neutralization dressed up as radical filmmaking, which might be worse than just making a bad movie because it makes you think the problem is already solved when it was never actually addressed.

texto: i believe my expectations were set too high for this film. and while i give merit to the aesthetic devices used to make this film, the lighting, cinematography, and music, this film was truly void of revolutionary political commentary or characterization. now, after reading other reviews on here, i understand that this was a complete falsified retelling of the main character’s true story. a man who was actually undercover for three years infiltrating black radical groups with the intention of causing the destabilization and downplay of their work. the writers picked apart and fabricated many parts of his story to make it seem like the main character and the police were fighting against racism. i mean, how inaccurate is this? the police, in rural colorado in the 70s, were working AGAINST the KKK? right. blatant copaganda and assimilation ideation. which makes sense given Spike Lee’s association with the NYPD, where they gave him over 200K for an ad campaign to promote relationships between the police and the black community. the characters seemed completely flat, what was Ron’s backstory? what were his motivations? why did Patrice get actively assaulted by a cop and then have no discussion about it? just a cut to an aestheticized montage. this was truly a disappointment on so many levels, not that we can expect radical media from large media corporations, but the premise seemed interesting while the film slowly descended into nonsense. especially the last scene at the bar with the cringe dialogue and arrest of the racist cop who had assaulted Patrice prior in the film, who was arrested on the grounds of saying racist shit? with that logic the entire KKK could have been rounded up an hour into the movie. painting the cops in a heroic light in a film about black subjugation and white violence is a fucking joke. and ending the film with a memoriam for a white white woman at the hands of white hatred instead of the thousands upon thousands of black and brown people killed by the systemic violence of the police? disgusting and tone deaf.

texto: I would like to start off by saying that as someone who really loved Do the Right Thing I was very excited to watch this movie. I mean, who wouldn't after reading that premise right? The sheer concept of a black cop infiltrating the KKK immediately got my attention...yet this film almost completely falls apart on every level. The first and last 5 minutes are great. The last scene with Ron and Patrice especially actually had me lock tf in, that was a powerful way to wrap the story up in a way I never expected. Everything else is kinda ass. I just wanna say that the editing in this movie is unironically one of the worst I've seen. The shots have absolutely no continuity after cutting, it keeps cutting in the most awkward moments, the genuinely powerful speech at the beginning has some really goofy closeups of the audience for some reason, there's just endless examples of atrocious editing that made it impossible for me to have fun with the film. This movie should have been a comedy, but for some reason it's a terrible one even with a premise this silly. There's nothing snappy about the intentionally comedic lines, it's just kind of awkwardly lumbering in its own rhythm and it's not funny. The acting is fine but nothing memorable. Adam Driver gave a better performance in Megalopolis of all things than this movie. The social commentary here also is just surface level as hell and cheap. It's genuinely shocking coming from the man behind one of the most nuanced movies on race tensions, that the main thing explored here is white people are racist. Any room for nuance set up by the plot of the movie: Adam Driver wrestling with his Jew heritage, Patrice's, and her people in general, hatred of cops, Ron's weird insistence on believing in changing the system from inside never truly being explored nor challenged, the racist cop(s) in Ron's department, and so much more are just...dropped? They don't reach anywhere close to resolution nor is there any development with these themes, they're just mentioned briefly and discarded. Why does Ron need to be on the phone? Why can't Adam Driver just be on the phone and meeting them in person? The premise itself has holes, and throughout the entire movie I honestly don't know what our characters are doing in the KKK. Do they really learn anything of value? Do I, the audience, even learn anything from watching this movie? There's not even like a comical examination of KKK's weird activities and procedures like I thought they would, it's like there's barely any research done into the organisation you're making a movie about. The whole movie is just Adam Driver and Ron dicking around in the KKK and hearing white people spam hate speech. It's not entertaining, funny, nor educational. It's cheap . The fucking 5 minutes KKK cutscene in Django Unchained with Quentin Tarantino as a racist Klan member was like a thousand times more entertaining than this movie in a fraction of its screentime.

texto: It's always a bit difficult to rate films based on true stories. It raises questions such as : should you aestheticize things that weren't ? Should a film's faithfulness to real events affect its rating ? Does it still need to be entertaining in the way it's directed ? In terms of pure feeling and a basic judgment, I can't help feeling that the film is wasted potential. It's only near the end that it comes close to the level of stress and tension that could have been present throughout the entire film, and it was only when real footage was shown for a few minutes that I felt genuinely hurt and outraged. Going back to the questions I raised at the beginning, I think the film tried too hard to stay entertaining and visually appealing, to the point of becoming almost comical by adding subtle humor to every scene and turning every character into a caricature. Or maybe white supremacists really were that ridiculous back then and I'm the one who's wrong ? But I think it's more likely a huge mistake on Spike Lee's part, combined with mid acting and mid direction. There's a serious lack of raw scenes showing the emotional struggles some of these characters may have gone through. The film almost gives the impression that social segregation wasn't all that violent, that racists were only a minority and that infiltrating a group of dangerous unstable sick individuals is just routine. And after a few quick searches, it becomes clear that the film is far from Ron Stallworth's real story. He first spent three years infiltrating black activists and radical black groups before infiltrating the KKK for nine months, not just one for a night and the other for a month. In conclusion, Spike Lee reduced reality to the story of a somewhat cool black cop infiltrating a group of somewhat stupid racists who do some not so nice things. But on the whole, it’s not a complete disaster with no substance or form. It’s just that looking at the film’s overall rating I get the impression that everyone has kind of agreed it’s a very good movie that represents the cause well. I suppose the intention was there, and the goal was still to highlight an important and underrepresented period of history, so let’s not be too harsh either.

On the surface you get a satisfying story where a Black cop infiltrates and disrupts the Klan. But that completely obscures the actual history that white supremacy wasn't ann external enemy. It was built into law enforcement and governance itself. The real problem is, it's neutralization dressed up as radical filmmaking, which might be worse than just making a bad movie because it makes you think the problem is already solved when it was never actually addressed.

It is not funny enough or ridiculous enough to work. It lacks a sense of urgency or tension that is required for quite a heavy subject matter. It is a shame it could've been quite great.

texto: Apesar de ter se tornado algo super politizado no final, eu ainda sim adorei o filme. Infiltrados na Klan é literalmente uma denúncia a "seitas" que ainda acontecem por pessoas da elite nos EUA, e é aquele tipo de filme que contém várias verdades "discretas", e situações que realmente ocorreram na vida real. Um ponto negativo é que o filme foi lançado justo em época de eleição, e eu senti que o criador tentou fazer da KKK uma ligação ao Trump, oque não faz sentido já que a KKK existe a mais de 50 anos. E pela história do policial ser realmente verídica, essa "ficção" faz toda a luta e investigação do policial parecer mentira. Mas entre toda via, este filme é importantíssimo, e conta uma história real da sociedade. E além disso, todo o preconceito e racismo que rola ao decorrer do filme, é só um espelho do que realmente acontece nesse confederado ridículo.

texto: 30 for 30: 2018 BlacKKKlansman✊🏿👻 This Spike Lee joint tells the story of two cops, one white and one black, that launch an operation to go undercover within the KKK. What comes out is a haunting yet still very relevant look at an America built on a racism. While I don’t think anything can ever top Do the Right Thing, I’m always seated for whatever this director puts out. I think what made that film an all timer for me is it asks a lot of questions about what is the “Right Thing”, particularly when it comes to inequality. I think this movie kind of builds on that theme, but amplifies it to a much higher degree with greater consequences. A fitting thing for when this movie came out that is still the same today. Politics are much more polarizing today. But, I also think Lee is much more unapologetic to excuses for racism than even his early films. The last 5 minutes of this lays it out clear. There are still limits to changing the system from within and hate has been on the rise again. Movie MVP: Going to go with Spike here. The director adds such a cool groove to this film that makes it feel both like a film in the 1970s, when it takes place, and in the late 2010s. It is bleak subject matter for sure, especially when the director uses real world examples of racial injustice and racism. Also really liked how the director challenged different forms of hate and how it should be tackled. Adam Driver’s character is just one example of this. He may not be visibly a target of racism, yet he is Jewish and would be the target of the same hate groups. There’s an interesting question in here of “well, why aren’t you doing more?” when fighting injustice that affects everyone. I think Spike does a good job of showing there are the good things that can come from working together to tackle such subjects. Favourite quotes: “You know the way to sell hate? Affirmative action, immigration, crime, tax reform, he says no one wants to be called a bigot anymore because Archie Bunker made that too uncool. So, the idea is under all these issues…everyday Americans can accept it. Support it. Until eventually, one day he gets somebody in the White House that embodies it.” “Sheeeeeeee-it!”

texto: A really good movie that I’d wanted to see for a long time. The performances are great, especially John David Washington and Adam Driver. One of the best parts of the movie is the unbelievable score. It’s incredible and works so well throughout. The undercover premise is fascinating, and the movie is genuinely funny while still dealing with a very serious topic. The shifts in tone actually work really well rather than feeling uneven. It also taught me quite a lot about the KKK, and the movie itself is very well made and shot. The final act is really strong, and the pacing throughout is excellent and I really love that ending. Overall, a fun, engaging and interesting movie with great performances, a fantastic score and a lot of strong elements. 8.4/10

texto: John David Washington is flexing his muscles here, but this is just as much Spike Lee showing off. That restless, slightly disorienting visual style somehow feels like the only way this story could've been told. The more ridiculous the narrative becomes, the more natural his direction feels. Also realised how musically driven his films are. I still can't quite work out how this became his biggest, though. Do the Right Thing deserves to be just as ubiquitous. Really wasn't prepared for that final sequence either. Lee has a knack for pulling the rug out from under you just when you think you've settled into his rhythm. If anything, it's only made me more excited to finally watch Malcolm X later this year.

texto: So well directed. But also so flawed. I’ll always be a fan of Spike Lee but he’s newer work really lacks the bite of his earlier work. Do the Right Thing and Malcolm X clear this. Some amazing sequences and humor but the thin line between fiction and reality and the cop-ness of it all really drags it down. The real life story is certainly compelling but the story decides to fictionalize some incredibly important aspects such as Flip’s identity, Ron’s personal philosophy, and Patrice. Patrice is the most frustrating part of all of this because she is an incredibly compelling character and her and Ron’s conversation about Blackxploitation films on the bridge is arguably one of the best scenes (shout out Shaft). If you’re going to tell a “true” story, don’t let the fictional stuff become more compelling than the real life story. This is clearly meant to be a response to modern politics and an analysis of the growth of political racism in the United States, which is incredibly compelling but it loses all credibility when the whole police department of an incredibly right wing town are all relatively supportive of the black guy (expect for the one guy but the writers clearly wanted a scapegoat). It’s just so frustrating because this is entertaining and well done but the political messaging of it is all over the place.

texto: Le Pape est mort. Au Vatican, un conclave se forme pour désigner qui succédera au Saint-Père. Structurellement composé de suspense, Conclave, nous plonge dans les coulisses de « l’Entreprise » la plus vieille au monde. La mise en scène d’Edward Berger installe une ambiance feutrée aux airs de Polar huit clos, porté par un casting international cohérent avec le propos, Ici ce n’est pas tant l’élection qui importe mais ce besoin de justesse que cherche sans fin le Cardinal Lawrence, joué par Ralph Fiennes. Sujet objectivement sensible, le film ne manquera pas d’évoquer les dernières casseroles que tirent l’Eglise, sans en faire le sous thème de son film. J’en retiens 20 minutes de trop, ralentissant un rythme déjà peu dynamique compte tenu de l’Arene (le Vatican) et de ses composants (les Cardinaux). Pas la plus grande révélation mais un sujet intéressant avec un vrai plus sur la mise en scène et la musique

texto: • This landed a bit below my expectations but it was still a fine, high-brow drama with tense moments, good music, and well-built characters. • Fiennes is astonishingly good in this movie, to the point that he outshines the likes of Lithgow and Tucci (but not Rossellini) in their scenes together • One thing I liked was that through all this nasty politics the reverence for the previous Pope (at least among his supporters) is clear. It’s as if the Pope can do no wrong, if anything was his doing, it becomes “okay”, and yet all the suitors for the next papacy are clearly prone to questionable decisions. • Cardinal Lawrence is perhaps a bit too pure, he is the protagonist but he doesn’t really show any impure notions the whole movie

texto: Num geral, é um filme bom, muito bem produzido, com ótimos personagens, atores, figurinos, críticas muito bem trabalhadas e construtivas, além de cenas de tensão muito boas. Porém, esse final do filme estraga TUDO. Colocar a revelação de que um cardeal hermafrodita foi escolhido pelo Conclave para ser o papa só para forçar mensagens políticamente ideológicas foi absurdo de ruim, e um enorme desrespeito com a igreja Católica de graça. Até eu que nem sou católico me ofendi com essa blasfêmia. Estragou o filme, então um honesto 5/10. (Além do que eu quase ia esquecendo de falar: esse papa foi eleito de forma apressada e sem nexo por causa de um discurso contra o cardeal Tedesco, simplesmente por reclamar dele estar utilizando a "ira" contra os terroristas Islâmicos que tinham atacado a igreja horas antes. Mesmo com as críticas sendo boas e necessárias, eu acho um exagero tratar o Tedesco como vilão do início ao fim do filme só por ele ser conservador).

texto: conclave isn’t bad at all, but this is genuinely one of the more disappointing movies i’ve watched. i went into it with pretty high expectations because the whole setup sounded SO interesting, and the movie definitely has the ingredients for something incredible. the Vatican setting, the secretive atmosphere, the politics, everyone hiding something… i was ready to be completely hooked. Ralph Fiennes was really good though, and i liked watching Cardinal Lawrence try to keep everything under control while slowly realizing that basically everyone around him has their own agenda. the whole process of the conclave was probably my favourite part because there’s this constant feeling that one little reveal could completely change everything. but the actual mystery just didn’t hit me as hard as i wanted it to. there were some twists that were interesting, but by the end i was more like “oh… okay” than completely shocked. i think that’s what disappointed me most because the movie spends so much time building up this huge sense of intrigue that i expected the payoff to absolutely destroy me. it’s still really well-made, the performances are strong and the atmosphere is great, but i just wanted MORE from it. maybe if i hadn’t gone in with such high expectations i’d feel differently.
