texto: Hacer una reseña de esta película es algo innecesario cuando ya tienes una reseña de la primera porque literalmente parecen la misma película, todos los elemento, ritmo, estética e identidad se transmite de una a otra, y aunque sé que Tarantino dice que son la misma película tampoco exageramos, es obvio que son películas distintas porque puedes notar como algunas aspectos se intensifican en esta segunda entrega, pero es todo en temas de edición y post producción porque más allá de eso si está madre estuviera pegada una con la otra sería una sola película. Lo que trato de decir es que es muy notorio que la intención original era tener un mega corte y no está división en dos partes, y el único motivo por el que estas dos película se sienten distintas es porque estos weyes vieron la recepción de la primera parte e intensificaron ciertos elementos en la edición del segundo volume, y bien por ellos porque todo salió nice. Algo que si puedo mencionar es que esta película es mucho más caricaturesca que la primera parte, lleva ciertos segmentos a puntos que has de cuenta estás viendo Naruto, pero también sucede algo similar con las escenas “serias” que se ven más fuertes y seriesonas, lo cual me lleva a pensar que todo esto es una consecuencia de que estamos en el clímax o final de la historia por lo que todas las escenas en general exageran con más intensidad todo. ¿Lo considero algo malo? No, pero es un cambio en el tono que no puedo ignorar y que quería mencionar porque podría ser cuestión de gusto o disgusto. Tipo el personaje de Pai Mei está en un borde muy peligroso para mí, aunque no lo logre atravesar. Siempre que se trata de una historia de venganza solemos tener este momento de “la venganza es mala” y la afrontación del dilema de obtener lo que quieres y sus consecuencias, y no es porque todos los escritores estén universalmente de acuerdo con ello, es porque narrativamente enfrentarte a un final que es exactamente lo que buscaba el personaje suele ser aburrido y anticlimqtico. Es claro desde la primera película que Tarantino no tiene intención alguna de meterse en esos dilemas y profundizar en sus personajes de esta forma, y no lo digo como algo malo, de hecho de cierta forma es valiente simplificar las cosas aquí, pero debo admitir que tras la muerte de Bill me habría gustado ver algo más, lo que sea, es para mi el único pero real que tengo con la película y es uno a medias porque siempre supe que iba ser así, hasta estoy contento que todo esa sección previa a la pelea con la hija estuviera ahí porque pudo haber sido peor. Lo que trato de decir es que haber conseguido exactamente lo que esperaba es similar a cuando consigue exactamente lo que quiere, ¿y después que? Me habría gustado ver algo más que un simple “ahora tiene a su hija y Bill está muerto”. Parece que estoy diciendo muchas quejas, pero la realidad no podría estar más lejos de ello. Kill Bill Vol. 2 me mamó y si hablo de dos cosas en específico que no me terminaron de convencer es solo gracias a que todo lo demás está súper bien. Tarantino puede ser un pendejo, pero el wey tiene salsa en los dedos y prepara pura obra culinaria.

texto: Good fun. Obviously it's not super deep or challenging but for a family science fiction, this is a good time. Leave it to pre-9/11 Barry Sonnenfeld to make a proper action comedy that anyone can enjoy. Speaking of which, the twin towers are just... ever-present in this. I can't help but to chuckle at the thought of families needing to pause Men In Black to explain fucking 9/11 to their kids. Hysterical. Better to learn about it from a movie and loving parents than some twisted conspiracy nut on the playground. The amount of misinformation I was fed by peers while growing up is staggering. I digress. Will Smith and Tommy Lee Jones have real chemistry and they work very well independently as well. They're simply a great duo and the single best part of this film. Edgar Suit Bug is a close second though. I LOVE Vincent D'Onofrio (I definitely fucked up that spelling, sorry Vince) in this. The raw physicality and deterioration of Edgar is amazing. The makeup/costume people knocked it out of the park. I loved Rip Torn in this as well. Shitty shitty shitty CGI. The practical effects in this were awwwwwwesome but the digital shit? Lost in Space grade. Even the CGI mouth on the pug looked like ass. If only they'd known how TERRIBLY it would age. Alas... Was this movie a little racist? Barry Sonnenfeld, nothing on God's Green Earth can make me forgive you for Nine Lives. MiB, though, is a welcomed part of our healing process. Five Mutzies and Glicks

texto: Tommy Lee Jones and Will Smith Star in I would argue some of their most iconic roles as J and K in 1997's men in black A funny and fun movie over all that I feel could have went a bit deeper into the world building aspect. Albeit at a tight 90 minute run time everything you need in this movie is already here, it really just boils down to personal preference. Would have liked to get more interaction with aliens just living their daily lives. Special effects are the way to do it here, a mix of practical with CGI (and it's that good pre 2000's CGI) all of the set pieces are fun and interesting, and the movie definitely has something to say about ones duty to the human race in terms of keeping the peace. However in recent years, shady government agencies with little to no oversight that are a complete secret from the public at large is something I'm inherently distrustful of (I understand this movie was of the times). Loved will smiths growth here and how he went from brightly colored outfits to the classic black suit. The giant cockroach alien as well scared the fuck out of me as a kid now I watch it and I laugh because of the camp and charm of this movie. Mother fucker literally walks like Frankenstein which I think was the point. Tommy Lee jones plays a very reserved role here, mentor like figure with no time for jokes and a past barely mentioned (because who you were before doesn't matter). Shame he got vored at the end but hey at least he got out and at least he doesn't remember it. Need to watch the sequels next. Would watch again but this for sure is not my favorite movie. Still trying to figure out what didn't land with me.

texto: Driven by the eccentric nature it embraces, the film pushes beyond conventional boundaries, but ultimately never reaches its undeniable limits. It’s one of those classic movies that is considered iconic because it started something new or elevated a past project, still iconic isn’t equivalent to good, appreciative but never good. Well, still it has some good qualities that seems never to be conducted In an essential trajectory. I absolutely like the chemistry between Tommy Lee jones and will smith, it truly indicates it’s kind of mentor and master relationship, it simply showcases the passing of the torch, combining their unique personas to generate somewhat a hilarious dynamic. I know it undisputedly trying to speculate some goofy shit, but it never seems to excite me in nearly every scene. I personally think it shares some Scooby-Doo esque qualities, but explores them through a more mature lens that never dignifies its eccentric and exhilarating structure with undue seriousness. It definitely thrives with complete and utter priority with how sophisticated visual composition are. Sculpting with identity rather than unimaginative style, benefiting the restorative design it features. Immensely overrated. Never flourishing in succeeding to genuinely showcase it’s premise with care, and undoubtedly cringy in some respects that I found myself just wanting to close my eyes. 4.7/10

texto: Schon seit Jahren leben unter Aufsicht einer (US-?!)Regierungsbehörde Aliens unter uns. Diese Behörden wird durch einen unorthodoxen Rookie verstärkt der direkt bei der Rettung der Erde unterstützen muss. Moderner Klassiker als klassisches Buddy-Movie, das sich durch schnelles Tempo, damals revolutionäre Effekte und großen Style-Willen auszeichnet. Ich bin kein Fan von Tommy Lee Jones und schon gar nicht von Will Smith, die Odd-Couple-Jokes sind also an mir verschwendet. Ebenso die schwarzen Anzüge, die doofen Sonnenbrillen und der ganze Retro-Futurismus-Klumpatsch. Am besten gefallen mir noch die Aliens, die sich als eher suspekte menschliche Charaktere tarnen und einige sehr witzige Dialogzeilen der Aliens. Den Kindern hat's gefallen, immerhin.

texto: I finally watched Men in Black for the first time. Obviously I knew how culturally significant and iconic it became, but unfortunately I never watched it as a kid, and I think that probably would’ve changed my experience with it quite a bit. I can definitely see the appeal, especially as a kids’ movie. The whole concept of aliens secretly living among humans disguised as normal people is really creative, and combining that with two agents hunting down aliens, weird gadgets and goofy humor makes for a fun ’90s premise. The concept was probably more interesting to me than the actual story, though. The plot just never really caught me. It basically comes down to them chasing a big alien who’s looking for a galaxy hidden on a cat’s collar, and the whole thing felt pretty random and messy to me. There wasn’t really a storyline or mystery that made me particularly curious about what was going to happen next. There are some funny moments, and Will Smith does his usual charismatic Will Smith thing, but nothing about the characters or story really stood out to me. The effects are also pretty decent considering this came out in 1997, even if they’ve obviously aged. Overall, I can appreciate Men in Black for what it is and understand why a lot of people who grew up with it still love it. It’s a goofy, creative and very ‘90s sci-fi action comedy that probably would’ve worked much better for me as a kid. I’m glad I finally watched such a big pop-culture classic, but I don’t really feel the need to watch it again anytime soon.

texto: James Edwards, a New York City police officer, encounters a suspect with unusual abilities and garners the attention of a secret government agency. He trades in his life to become Agent J and learns all about the undergroup extraterrestrial market. There is a particularly dangerous bug that causes intergalactic turmoil and war. Agents K and J try to get rid of the bug and maintain intergalactic diplomacy. Somehow, there is both a lot and a little to unpack here; the whole world of aliens hiding in plain sight is a clever setup, and the film does a good job sticking to its own rules. However, there is nothing speculative here, nor is there any allegory. I know it’s supposed to be fun, but there seems to be little to no tone or atmosphere. Everything in this film is built for a quick popcore experience, flashy effects, and little depth. Nothing was offensive, and I can't pinpoint anything that actively detracted from my enjoyment. I guess I just didn’t love it. Will Smith and Tommy Lee Jones bounce off each other, and their chemistry is fine, but it’s not my favorite buddy-cop pairing. The action sequences are fine, but the agents feel more like superheroes than law enforcement. How am I supposed to believe that these “bugs” are so tough and such a threat when Will Smith effectively wins a one-on-one fist fight? There’s spectacle and wit, but I guess MiB just didn’t hit home this time.

tema: Efeitos práticos e design de criaturas
exemplo: Reviews elogiam os efeitos práticos e o design de criaturas, mesmo que reconheçam que a tecnologia deixa um pouco a desejar em comparação com filmes modernos.
texto: Ce n’est clairement pas la première fois que je regarde Men in Black, et même après plusieurs visionnages, je trouve que le film fonctionne toujours aussi bien. Je lui mets 4/5, parce que c’est un film qui a beau avoir pris quelques années, il garde un charme et une efficacité que j’apprécie énormément. Déjà, le duo Will Smith et Tommy Lee Jones est clairement l’un des gros points forts du film. J apporte toute l’énergie, l’humour et la curiosité du personnage qui découvre complètement cet univers, tandis que K est l’exact opposé : il est blasé, sérieux et donne l’impression d’avoir absolument tout vu dans sa vie. Leur dynamique est vraiment excellente et permet au film d’enchaîner les moments sérieux avec des scènes beaucoup plus absurdes sans que ça paraisse forcé. Et puis il faut quand même parler du concept : une organisation secrète qui surveille les extraterrestres vivant parmi nous, efface la mémoire des témoins et règle les problèmes avant même que le grand public ne comprenne ce qui s’est passé. Franchement, leur méthode de travail est particulière. « Vous venez de voir un extraterrestre ? » FLASH. « Quel extraterrestre ? » Pratique, mais niveau respect de la vie privée, on repassera. J’aime énormément la façon dont le film nous fait découvrir cet univers à travers J. Au départ, il ne croit évidemment pas à tout ça et pense simplement avoir affaire à quelque chose d’inexplicable. Puis il découvre progressivement que les extraterrestres existent réellement, qu’ils sont partout et que certains ressemblent suffisamment aux humains pour vivre totalement normalement parmi nous. C’est probablement ce qui rend l’univers aussi amusant : tout peut être extraterrestre et personne ne le sait. Le film mélange également très bien science-fiction, action et comédie. Il y a de vraies scènes d’action, des enjeux et même quelques passages assez impressionnants, mais l’ensemble ne se prend jamais totalement au sérieux. C’est justement ce qui fait son charme. Les créatures sont d’ailleurs toujours aussi amusantes à regarder. Les effets spéciaux ont évidemment vieilli depuis 1997, mais personnellement ça ne me dérange pas énormément. Au contraire, je trouve que certains effets pratiques donnent encore aujourd’hui un charme particulier au film. On sent davantage le travail effectué sur les créatures et les costumes, là où certains films modernes peuvent parfois devenir tellement dépendants du numérique qu’on perd un peu cette sensation de « réel ». J’aime également beaucoup l’esthétique du film. Les costumes noirs, les lunettes de soleil, les voitures, les gadgets et cette ambiance très années 90 donnent immédiatement une identité aux Men in Black. Même sans voir le titre, quelques secondes suffisent pour reconnaître l’univers. Et évidemment, il y a toutes ces petites scènes absurdes qui font que le film reste aussi divertissant. Parce qu’on parle quand même de types en costard qui peuvent passer leur journée à gérer des extraterrestres, des armes capables de faire exploser absolument n’importe quoi et des créatures géantes… tout en gardant un calme professionnel. Moi, après avoir vu une bestiole sortir d’un endroit où elle n’avait absolument rien à faire, je pense que j’aurais demandé une mutation. Le scénario reste malgré tout assez simple et certains éléments sont aujourd’hui beaucoup plus prévisibles. On sent également que le film appartient à son époque, notamment dans son rythme et certains effets. Mais honnêtement, je ne regarde pas Men in Black pour avoir un scénario extrêmement complexe. Je le regarde parce que c’est fun, drôle, efficace et extrêmement reconnaissable. Et puis Will Smith apporte énormément au film. Il possède cette capacité à rendre son personnage drôle sans avoir besoin d’en faire constamment des tonnes. C’est naturellement amusant parce qu’il réagit exactement comme nous réagirions probablement dans certaines situations : avec beaucoup trop de questions et probablement un peu de panique intérieure. Au final, Men in Black reste pour moi un très bon divertissement et surtout un film qui a une vraie personnalité. Il n’est peut-être plus aussi impressionnant techniquement qu’à sa sortie, mais son humour, son duo principal, son univers et son ambiance fonctionnent encore très bien. Un film que je peux clairement revoir avec plaisir. Et si jamais les extraterrestres existent vraiment… j’espère simplement que les Men in Black font bien leur travail, parce que personnellement, je n’ai aucune envie de découvrir ce qui vit réellement dans les égouts de New York.

texto: La premisa es una genialidad: la Tierra es básicamente la terminal de retiro pero del universo, llena de bichos intergalácticos camuflados laburando de puesteros, perros que hablan y viejos que resultan ser robots manejados por un alien minúsculo adentro de la cabeza, me hubiera gustado ver reptilianos, pero nos dieron cucarachoides jaja, el antepasado de los Kukas. De chico me acuerdo patente que la vi y me dejó un trauma hermoso: me dio un cagazo tremendo matar cucarachas, fijo yo pisaba una y pensaba que me iba a ir abducido y usado de encubadora de aliens. Pero la escena cumbre, la que me define al personaje de Will Smith como mi pj favorito sin precedentes, es la prueba de tiro con los milicos de elite. Los otros mamertos disparándole a monstruos de cartón que estaban estornudando y el chabón le mete un corchazo limpio entre ceja y ceja a la nena. Cuando le piden explicaciones tira cátedra pura: "Y entonces vi a la pequeña Tiffany. Y pensé: una niña blanca de 8 años, en medio del gueto, rodeada de monstruos, a esta hora de la noche, ¿con libros de física cuántica? ¡Esa perra tramaba algo, Zed! Tiene como 8 años, esos libros son demasiado avanzados para ella. Si me pregunta, yo digo que tramaba algo." Es cine, hermano. Efectos prácticos que envejecieron como los dioses, humor negro en su punto justo y el bicho espacial sufriendo como loco mientras le revientan los huevos a chancletazos. Dame diez de estas antes que cualquier porquería con pantalla verde de hoy en día.

texto: It’s been many years since I last watched Men in Black, and revisiting it reminded me just how fun it is. It’s a non‑serious sci‑fi comedy in which Will Smith plays a cop recruited into the Men in Black, a secret agency tasked with monitoring alien activity and managing what the public sees and remembers. The film thrives on deadpan humour and absurd alien encounters, and its comedic tone is one of its strongest features. It never pretends to be serious sci‑fi: instead, it leans into its own silliness with confidence. The dynamic between Agent J (James) and Agent K is the film’s emotional centre. K’s stoic professionalism, interspersed with dry sarcasm, contrasts perfectly with J’s energetic, reactive presence. J feels like a genuine apprentice, inexperienced but clearly capable, and their chemistry gives the film a likeable set of protagonists. I enjoyed the world: aliens living disguised among humans, an entire hidden ecosystem ticking away beneath everyday life, and the Men in Black quietly keeping it all in order. The MIB headquarters, the gadgets, and the neuralyzer are iconic touches, and the creature effects hold up visually — especially Edgar the Bug once he reveals his true form. The film isn’t driven by heavy themes, but there are hints worth noting: the personal cost of secrecy, shown through Agent K’s distant relationship with his former love, and the playful reminder of cosmic insignificance — that humanity is just one small part of a much larger universe. It’s a brisk watch, but never feels rushed. Plenty happens, and the pacing keeps the film light and engaging. For me, it remains a defining Will Smith comedy and a cornerstone of 90s sci‑fi cinema. A solid, enjoyable 7/10.

J’aime énormément la façon dont le film nous fait découvrir cet univers à travers J. Au départ, il ne croit évidemment pas à tout ça et pense simplement avoir affaire à quelque chose d’inexplicable. Puis il découvre progressivement que les extraterrestres existent réellement, qu’ils sont partout et que certains ressemblent suffisamment aux humains pour vivre totalement normalement parmi nous. C’est probablement ce qui rend l’univers aussi amusant : tout peut être extraterrestre et personne ne le sait. Le film mélange également très bien science-fiction, action et comédie. Il y a de vraies scènes d’action, des enjeux et même quelques passages assez impressionnants, mais l’ensemble ne se prend jamais totalement au sérieux. C’est justement ce qui fait son charme. Les créatures sont d’ailleurs toujours aussi amusantes à regarder. Les effets spéciaux ont évidemment vieilli depuis 1997, mais personnellement ça ne me dérange pas énormément. Au contraire, je trouve que certains effets pratiques donnent encore aujourd’hui un charme particulier au film. On sent davantage le travail effectué sur les créatures et les costumes, là où certains films modernes peuvent parfois devenir tellement dépendants du numérique qu’on perd un peu cette sensation de « réel ». J’aime également beaucoup l’esthétique du film. Les costumes noirs, les lunettes de soleil, les voitures, les gadgets et cette ambiance très années 90 donnent immédiatement une identité aux Men in Black. Même sans voir le titre, quelques secondes suffisent pour reconnaître l’univers. Et évidemment, il y a toutes ces petites scènes absurdes qui font que le film reste aussi divertissant. Parce qu’on parle quand même de types en costard qui peuvent passer leur journée à gérer des extraterrestres, des armes capables de faire exploser absolument n’importe quoi et des créatures géantes… tout en gardant un calme professionnel. Moi, après avoir vu une bestiole sortir d’un endroit où elle n’avait absolument rien à faire, je pense que j’aurais demandé une mutation. Le scénario reste malgré tout assez simple et certains éléments sont aujourd’hui beaucoup plus prévisibles. On sent également que le film appartient à son époque, notamment dans son rythme et certains effets. Mais honnêtement, je ne regarde pas Men in Black pour avoir un scénario extrêmement complexe. Je le regarde parce que c’est fun, drôle, efficace et extrêmement reconnaissable. Et puis Will Smith apporte énormément au film. Il possède cette capacité à rendre son personnage drôle sans avoir besoin d’en faire constamment des tonnes. C’est naturellement amusant parce qu’il réagit exactement comme nous réagirions probablement dans certaines situations : avec beaucoup trop de questions et probablement un peu de panique intérieure. Au final, Men in Black reste pour moi un très bon divertissement et surtout un film qui a une vraie personnalité. Il n’est peut-être plus aussi impressionnant techniquement qu’à sa sortie, mais son humour, son duo principal, son univers et son ambiance fonctionnent encore très bien. Un film que je peux clairement revoir avec plaisir. Et si jamais les extraterrestres existent vraiment… j’espère simplement que les Men in Black font bien leur travail, parce que personnellement, je n’ai aucune envie de découvrir ce qui vit réellement dans les égouts de New York.

I loved all the characters and there were so many sweet moments packed into 90 minutes. The film really has something special about it that I think a lot of 90s/00s films had - freedom of expression. So many films these days feel like they’re forcibly injected with some moral message or they tell a narrative about how bad the world is nowadays, but back then it felt like films existed for films sake. The story that is being told is held inside the bubble of the world the film chooses to portray. It was easier to get lost in the film because it wasn’t constantly trying to send some grand message to the audience. Big fan

texto: Time / distance and a shit-crusted legacy have tainted this a little but it shouldn't be forgotten that separated from its monumentally awful 2002 sequel , its vastly improved heavily belated 2012 quasi-reboot-sequel and its dead-eyed and embarrassing 2019 ' legacy sequel ' this thing was absolutely huge - culturally, cinematically and of course financially (pulling in over $589.3 million worldwide on a $90 million budget). It takes the tone GHOSTBUSTERS expertly birthed over a decade earlier and builds out from there with charismatic and talented movie stars, a truly smart and knowing screenplay, tremendous set-pieces and utterly fabulous Rick Baker's alien creature designs... ... it creates an entire 'in world' construct, established rules and conventions within it, conflict, character development and ~insane~ narrative propulsion all within a staggeringly impressive, lean as hell 90 odd minutes. It isn't just one of the best blockbusters of its decade, it's one of the best of all time.

texto: "Sabermetrics" is the application of statistical analysis to baseball records, esp. in order to evaluate and compare the performance of individual players. The definition alone puts most people to sleep, and yet they made a movie about it. So if you haven't watch any of the trailers and don't know anything about it, Moneyball is the true story of Billy Beane (Brad Pitt), the manager of the Oakland A's who used the sabermetrics concept to stay within his ghetto Oakland budget in order to get a decent team. All the good players like Jason Giambi and Johnny Damon, after 2001, went on to play respectively for the Yankees and the Red Sox, the two most annoying and also wealthiest teams in the American league. In order to replace the star players, Billy Beane, with the help of Jonah Hill (who's character I don't know is fictional or not), crunched a bunch of numbers together to scout out the players that looked bad on paper, but because they statistically got on base a lot more, would be worth buying. This wasn't exactly a feel-good movie about how Beane used a revolutionary new method of scouting and brought a team to victory. Because, let's face it, does anyone remember Oakland winning a World Series any time since 1989? Hell no! Beane is still the GM of the A's and still, they suck big clanking moneyballs. But, the movie isn't about that. Aaron Sorkin, who co-wrote the screenplay, is a genius at getting a different message across. The Social Network wasn't about the invention of Facebook, it was about a nerdy guy who made a lot of complicated choices to become who he was. Moneyball is really about a guy who just tries a different philosophy. When Beane was in high school, the scouts all said he'd be a star player and convinced him to give up a Stanford scholarship to play for the Mets, but he bottomed out. As it's pointed out in Moneyball, this happens all the time. Not even just in baseball, but in most sports. Scouts really don't know jack shit about how a player is going to develop, so why not try this way? It seemed a perfect fit for Beane, who's portrayed by Pitt as a guy who wants badly to not have anything human to do with the players. He didn't want to have to get to know them, less he has to fire or trade them. He'd rather base everything on numbers, let the cold facts make the decisions for him. He struggles with it until he understand that you can't take romance about of baseball. These are human beings, not predictable machines, and Baseball is so ingrained in the American psyche as an escapist pastime that most people aren't going to easily accept something like sabermetrics. I liked Moneyball more than I thought I would. I didn't think there would be any point to basing a movie on something that didn't work. Hey, let's next do a movie on the development of New Coke! But, the theme sold me, and then so did Pitt's performance. Even Jonah Hill was good, not playing the sarcastic fat guy he's known for. I was hoping to see more of Oakland, but I mostly got scenes of that ghetto Coliseum, and all those shipyard structures, but that's just me. I shouldn't have expected Lake Merritt or something. The movie did last a long time so if you're not at all into baseball or the story, you might be looking at your watch.

texto: Prestige (derogatory). Operates very well on a whole bunch of levels with nothing too complex to actually say. Aaron Sorkin credit roll made a lot of things make sense retroactively (kept thinking Brad Pitt looked like him with that hair cut). Mostly the melodramatic temper tantrums and the childishly aggro and egoic social-verbal posturing. Engaging but not sustaining? That is to say the film has the bones to hang ideas from but pretty sparse meat and connective tissue. Also, there are no women in this movie who are people. Absolutely bored out of my gourd during all the trite family drama. Would have been stronger if the family had depth or their total one dimensionality was examined as it relates to the protagonist’s subjectivity. As it was, cloying and or unremarkable ciphers and cliches employed competently toward banally rank ends. On the subject of under utilized and developed characters, far too little Hoffman. I kept waiting for them to give him more to do and they never did. Overall idk. Looked great on film. Novel to see archival footage blended up with new stuff and used to tell the story. Lotta textural medium stuff I enjoyed. And of course how can you not be romantic about baseball?

texto: I was pretty disappointed with this one. I really love baseball, I love the rhythm of it, the empty moments, I love how the unique focus the sport has on the individual, while each one having to deal with the consequences or reaping the rewards of a teammates good at bat. I love the sound of the crack of a bat, the feeling of a ball in one's glove, its a really beautiful sport. The social aspects of watching it and the absolute marathon that a season is are all things I've grown to really appreciate. Sadly I don't really know what any of this has to do with this movie. This is a boy movie, a I feel smart boy movie all about one-upping people with math and being emotionally closed off and punching walls movie. It just all around really is not for me. The story of the Oakland A's at this time is neat, its cool that such an undervalued team was able to play the numbers and do well in a season. It's very cool that the style of get guys on base no matter how changed baseball strategies. I just didn't really gel with the performances or the way that this narrative was told. Brad Pitt really does not do it for me in this one, he's so closed off and shit eating grinning all the time it got pretty boring. I feel like Philip Seymour Hoffman is devastatingly under-utilized. Getting a man as talented as that in your film and having him just be a peeved coach with almost no screen time is an incredible let down. I cannot believe that Jonah Hill was the actor and character I enjoyed most, and got the most out of watching. His performance as a young kid in the industry who knows what he's saying but doesn't have the courage to speak it and relying on Billy to do so works very well! I am a huge huge fan of the use of real baseball footage, and the actors who play the players were cast tremendously and do a spectacular job making the transition to real footage completely seamless. The quiet moments where Billy is around the A's ballpark were when I really liked the film.

In order to replace the star players, Billy Beane, with the help of Jonah Hill (who's character I don't know is fictional or not), crunched a bunch of numbers together to scout out the players that looked bad on paper, but because they statistically got on base a lot more, would be worth buying. This wasn't exactly a feel-good movie about how Beane used a revolutionary new method of scouting and brought a team to victory. Because, let's face it, does anyone remember Oakland winning a World Series any time since 1989? Hell no! Beane is still the GM of the A's and still, they suck big clanking moneyballs. But, the movie isn't about that. Aaron Sorkin, who co-wrote the screenplay, is a genius at getting a different message across. The Social Network wasn't about the invention of Facebook, it was about a nerdy guy who made a lot of complicated choices to become who he was. Moneyball is really about a guy who just tries a different philosophy. When Beane was in high school, the scouts all said he'd be a star player and convinced him to give up a Stanford scholarship to play for the Mets, but he bottomed out. As it's pointed out in Moneyball, this happens all the time. Not even just in baseball, but in most sports. Scouts really don't know jack shit about how a player is going to develop, so why not try this way? It seemed a perfect fit for Beane, who's portrayed by Pitt as a guy who wants badly to not have anything human to do with the players. He didn't want to have to get to know them, less he has to fire or trade them. He'd rather base everything on numbers, let the cold facts make the decisions for him. He struggles with it until he understand that you can't take romance about of baseball. These are human beings, not predictable machines, and Baseball is so ingrained in the American psyche as an escapist pastime that most people aren't going to easily accept something like sabermetrics. I liked Moneyball more than I thought I would. I didn't think there would be any point to basing a movie on something that didn't work. Hey, let's next do a movie on the development of New Coke! But, the theme sold me, and then so did Pitt's performance. Even Jonah Hill was good, not playing the sarcastic fat guy he's known for. I was hoping to see more of Oakland, but I mostly got scenes of that ghetto Coliseum, and all those shipyard structures, but that's just me. I shouldn't have expected Lake Merritt or something. The movie did last a long time so if you're not at all into baseball or the story, you might be looking at your watch.

texto: I don't know anything about baseball, but how can you not be romantic about it? Like, genuinely. If you asked me to explain the rules right now, I'd probably embarrass myself. However, Moneyball was actually pretty fucking good. A big part of why I enjoyed it is obviously Brad Pitt. I think he's officially one of my favourite actors at this point, so putting him in basically anything is already giving the movie a head start. He genuinely carries this really well. Billy Beane is such an interesting character because he's constantly trying to prove something to himself. He keeps raising the bar even when the bar is already fucking low, and no matter what he achieves, he's never completely satisfied. That ambition is both his biggest strength and probably his biggest weakness. He's so obsessed with finding the next way to improve that he doesn't really know when to stop. He's always chasing the next goal, trying to prove that his ideas can work and refusing to accept that things have to be done the way they've always been done. Then you've got Jonah Hill playing a serious role, which is bloody weird to see at first. I'm so used to him being the comedic relief that seeing him actually play someone more reserved and serious took me a minute, but he genuinely does a great job here, and the fact that he's not constantly trying to make you laugh actually makes his character work. The craziest part is that this is based on a true story. I know absolutely fuck all about baseball, but even I could appreciate how insane it is that these people were basically trying to change the way the sport was approached by looking at things differently. Sports, but online, using only statistics? I don't think I suddenly understand baseball now, but if someone asks me about it from this point onwards, Moneyball is basically going to be my entire knowledge of the sport.

texto: Moneyball is a baseball drama starring Brad Pitt as Billy Beane, the general manager of the Oakland A’s back in the early 2000s. The story signifies how Billy tried to build a competitive team despite having one of the smallest budgets in baseball. I feel like I saw this in bits and pieces a while ago, but I’m so glad to have watched it for a second time. If you are a sports or baseball fan I really think you would enjoy this film. On the other hand, if you don’t really care about baseball, some of the statistical/roster discussions are gonna feel dry. To be honest, most of the movie would feel dry to you because the main priority isn’t triumphant wins or thrilling scenes. The focus is more of a character/strategy drama than a conventional sports plot. Lots of dialogue and conversations surrounding the ball house. To me that doesn’t matter because the dialogue is sharp and the movie has a really good sense of momentum regardless of the stats.  I think it was really cool to witness the process of how the A’s were like a bottom of the barrel team to going on an insane win streak. You can’t give up on this film and have to stay till the end too. It’s an underdog story, but not the typical “team comes together and wins” story. If you’ve ever seen Major League, this is almost a serious version of that movie.The acting was top tier too. Brad Pitt is excellent as Beane with his smooth, charming demeanor and never giving up. Jonah Hill is great too in a more restrained dramatic role. I think the casting was awesome with how they put Pitt and Hill as the one two. Even if you don’t love baseball I think you should still give this a try. You can understand the basic concept of trying to accomplish more with less money. Although this is a safe hit of a movie, it’s always go Redsox baby.

texto: Moneyball is a baseball drama starring Brad Pitt as Billy Beane, the general manager of the Oakland A’s back in the early 2000s. The story signifies how Billy tried to build a competitive team despite having one of the smallest budgets in baseball. I feel like I saw this in bits and pieces a while ago, but I’m so glad to have watched it for a second time. If you are a sports or baseball fan I really think you would enjoy this film. On the other hand, if you don’t really care about baseball, some of the statistical/roster discussions are gonna feel dry. To be honest, most of the movie would feel dry to you because the main priority isn’t triumphant wins or thrilling scenes. The focus is more of a character/strategy drama than a conventional sports plot. Lots of dialogue and conversations surrounding the ball house. To me that doesn’t matter because the dialogue is sharp and the movie has a really good sense of momentum regardless of the stats.  I think it was really cool to witness the process of how the A’s were like a bottom of the barrel team to going on an insane win streak. You can’t give up on this film and have to stay till the end too. It’s an underdog story, but not the typical “team comes together and wins” story. If you’ve ever seen Major League, this is almost a serious version of that movie.The acting was top tier too. Brad Pitt is excellent as Beane with his smooth, charming demeanor and never giving up. Jonah Hill is great too in a more restrained dramatic role. I think the casting was awesome with how they put Pitt and Hill as the one two. Even if you don’t love baseball I think you should still give this a try. You can understand the basic concept of trying to accomplish more with less money. Although this is a safe hit of a movie, it’s always go Redsox baby.

texto: On the surface, this is an underdog story about a baseball team trying to compete with teams that have far more money and resources than they do. But underneath that, it’s such an interesting insight into a side of sport we rarely get to see. The finances, recruitment, statistics and decisions being made behind the scenes are just as important as what eventually happens on the field. What makes it even more interesting watching it now is knowing how much sport has changed since. The kind of data-driven thinking Billy is fighting to introduce has become such a huge part of modern sport, not just baseball. Analytics, finding value in players and trying to gain an advantage through information are now completely normal. You’re basically watching an approach that people thought was ridiculous become part of how modern sport operates. Then there’s Billy himself and the resistance he faces trying to change something that has been done the same way for decades. Everyone around him has their own idea of what a baseball player should look like and how a team should be built, because experience has taught them that’s simply how it works. Billy doesn’t have the money to play by those same rules, so he has to question whether the rules actually make sense in the first place. I really liked that idea. Just because something has always been done a certain way doesn’t mean it’s the best way of doing it. There’s something quite inspiring about watching someone believe in an idea while almost everyone around them is telling them it won’t work. Change means being willing to adapt, evolve and sometimes go against what everyone else accepts as normal. You might not even be the person who ultimately benefits the most from that change, but you can still be the person who proves that another way is possible.

texto: “How can you not be romantic about baseball?” That line, delivered by Brad Pitt’s Billy Beane after watching Jeremy Brown trip and stumble back to first base after him hitting a home run, is the moment I keep coming back to every time I watch Moneyball. I gave it five out five stars. I grew up with this story because baseball has been such a huge part of my life, and still is because I’m still playing. I also believe this is Brad Pitt and Jonah Hill’s most underrated and underappreciated work. Both performances carry the film without ever feeling like they’re reaching for attention. It feels very authentic. What I find just as compelling is Billy's relationship with his own scouting team. He gets annoyed at them for judging players purely on the eye test, even though that’s the exact same way he was scouted and brought into the league himself. It’s a strange contradiction, but it’s part of what makes his character work so well for me. Beyond the performances, I think the moneyball movement itself was the most impactful moment in the history of sports. It wasn’t just about analytics changing how teams evaluate players, it was about teaching big organizations across every sport that thinking unconventionally could actually win. That idea is bigger than baseball, and it’s a big part of why this movie has stuck with me for as long as it has.n

texto: The most advanced underdog sports movie of all time Moneyball is not a movie about the oakland athletics and their historic season, it's not a movie about the beauty of math and statistics, it's not even a movie about billy beane- the man who accomplished all this, it's a movie from billy beane. The entire film it told through his perspective and ideology, the games themselves, the actual baseball that is being played is an almost negligible part of the film, all we ever get to see in great detail is the outcome of each match, as beane did. Moneyball doesn't try to show you a baseball game and have you understand why something the players are doing is good or bad, it simplifies the sport down to a binary outcome- winning or losing, everything that happens in between those two outcomes is irrelevant. The movie has a way of making you feel like a middle aged baseball general manager, its so incredibly immersive that every feeling that beane has is reflected in the audience, it's what makes the film such a romantic affair- it's entire philosophy is developed around trying to understand a man who's romantic about baseball

texto: — the kind that makes spreadsheets and sabermetrics feel as tense as a ninth-inning at-bat. Bennett Miller frames it less like a sports movie and more like a heist film where the score being cased is a full season, and it plays almost like the spiritual predecessor to Ted Lasso: an outsider's unconventional method quietly dismantling an entrenched system. The scene of Jonah Hill walking Brad Pitt through his numbers is the film's clearest thesis statement, and the camera knows it — pushing in tight enough that you can see the pixels on the screen, the data itself becoming the emotional core of the scene. That's the trick of the whole movie: turning cold math into something that comes alive. Pitt and Hill's chemistry does a lot of the heavy lifting too, Billy's practiced confidence playing off Peter's shy, introverted uncertainty in a way that never feels like odd-couple shtick. And Billy Beane's backstory isn't just texture — it's the engine underneath everything, the reason his refusal to accept mediocrity reads as compulsion rather than strategy: a guy who was once the sure thing that didn't pan out, demanding the best from everyone else because he never got to demand it from himself, and never extending that kindness back to the players under him. Even the smaller touches land — the American flag catching the light on the diamond, the surprise of seeing Liverpool's John Henry pop up as a cameo when you already bleed red for that club. There isn't a ton left to say about it at this point except that it's fully earned its status as a cult classic of the genre.

texto: You could say I’ve found myself in a Double Bind. I’m incredibly torn on this. The film is both undoubtedly ahead of its time and deeply of its time. It has a complete and total understanding of fandom and stan culture most contemporary films should be jealous of, before either had even been born let alone matured to what they are now. The psychological examination of Mima is fascinating and the film abandons all tradition when it comes to structure to force its audience into her perspective and feel as though you’re losing your mind along with her. However, in the twisty third act that level of intense scrutiny when it comes to Mima’s psychology is left by the wayside. I’m not a fan of the Rumi twist. When a film is entirely about the inner workings of someone’s mind and then suddenly decides to be about someone else’s sudden mental break I’m just left a little annoyed. It’s not even that it feels like it comes out of nowhere but that it’s so much less interesting. Suddenly the film is about a bitter, older, fatter woman desperately deluding herself as she cloys for the attention a younger, prettier, thinner girl is getting. A played out trope that’s usage here borders on misogynistic? Mima’s struggle isn’t about perfection (which is why the claim Black Swan ripped this movie off beat for best makes no sense to me, clearly took inspiration but the cores are so different) it’s about identity. So the personification of her struggle with identity no longer being a part of her but someone else seems to undermine that journey. Especially, because once Rumi is revealed, the film ends and Mima is perfectly fine and self assured again. I just feel underwhelmed. Something so interesting becomes so dull. It feels like the film is dedicated to trying to tell an earnest story about being a woman in the spotlight and in some places it succeeds but in others it feels like it falls directly in line with what it’s trying to critique. I’m not someone that thinks rape or sexual assault should never be depicted. Artists have a right to create art about anything they want to. These things are real so of course there should be stories about them. And while the sexual assault and rape scenes (whether real ir acted) are intentionally disturbing in an affective way, they also seem to be drawn and directed in such a way to titillate the viewer. Now, I understand that this is a film about voyeurism and it’s absolutely drenched in metaphor. I don’t think this is just some misogynistic torture porn it’s not that simple. I think it tries to be a story exposing the horrific reality many women face, whether that be the threat of sexual violence or being pressured and pushed into uncomfortable situations or society’s crazymaking obsession with youth and fame and attention being forced upon them. I think in some places it succeeds and in some places it fails. Part of me thinks a big reason why this has the reputation it does is because it’s an anime and if this same film were made in live action there would be less fondness for it. And I mean it is a very well animated film although not much differentiates it from most anime I’ve seen on a technical level. On a thematic level I think everything here is pushing towards a cohesive whole. Every element has something to do with fame and audience and compromise and voyeurism and obsession. There is a thematic throughline here that is definite. But that seems to come at the expense of a throughline for our narrative and characters. Which I’m often more than happy to look past but here so much of this film is built around character. It’s almost a character study of Mima for most of its runtime. texto: There’s some thought provoking themes about perception of self, self growth, and fame. Mina’s transition from pop star to actress is extremely messy. texto: quite a trippy and confusing film but it was good and different from a lot of films I've seen. it's a film that discusses explicitly how much control the patriarchy has over women, and esp how women in the entertainment industry barely have any control over themselves and what they want to do, that doesn't matter to the industry, everything mira "agrees" to hurts her, mentally and physically, she is used and sexualised and only agrees to it bc she feels she has to, "this is just a part of the business" and she doesn't really realise that she can say no, not that it would matter if she did. this lack of care ntrol she has spirals throughout the film as she has no idea whats going on anymore, what she's done and can't distinguish dreams from reality, emphasising how little control she has over her own life, so much that it's barely even hers anymore and she just tunes in at random moments. and the ending shows how men's "ownership" of women in the industry has always been happening, rumi represents what mira could have become, and rumis persona being pop idol mira clearly shows how much being a pop idol herself with all the expectations affected rumi, while she was not successful like mira was she still clung onto her past bc it is likely when she felt the most desired in an industry and world where approval (esp from men) is key to success, (and who doesn't want to be loved/adored?) so she separated herself as she is from who she used to be/wanted to be as a way of coping (and I think that she also experienced sexual assault like mira did, which definitely impacted her, I think esp bc of her reaction to mira doing the tape scene). however, since it did have a few scenes of sexual assault (one in an acting setting but still) and personally I don't like seeing those in media I don't think I will be watching this film again but it does a very deep dive into the horror of the exploitation of women in the entertainment industry.

tema: Tema da identidade e da obsessão
exemplo: O filme aborda de forma intensa a luta da protagonista contra a percepção que os outros têm dela, assim como a obsessão do fã que se torna uma ameaça real, explorando a psicologia de personagens e o preço da fama.
texto: A beautiful, astonishingly well-written exploration of the objectification of pop stars, the paranoia inherent to being a celebrity and being surrounded by potential enemies at all times, the psychological effects of being a woman and being surrounded by larger men who would be more than happy to rape you if the opportunity presented itself, the difference between our professional and personal personas and the troubles that can arise if those boundaries blur, and the jealousy older women have for younger women once their sexual value has subsided, all of it set at the dawn of the Internet (which has turned us all into mini-celebrities to some degree). I must confess at the outset that one of my big life goals is to become a pornographer. I've never wanted children, and after a few lucrative decades spent training for and then succeeding at high-paying Silicon Valley tech jobs, I am restless to spend my thirties becoming physically strong and sexually virile. I want to become extremely strong and create an OnlyFans where I make love to a succession of beautiful, ideally white, young women in both conventional and comedic scenarios, filmed POV. There's not much profit in it, but frankly, I already have enough money (for myself to live off, so don't get any bright ideas that I'm Richie Rich). The whole point of making money is to ultimately be able to do what you want with your life. Some men want to race cars, others to raise large families, others to hunt and fish. I want to direct adult films and be a stud. (I also have higher-minded, more conventional artistic goals as relates to my own people, the Hindus, but those might be more of a later-life thing. I have time.) I tell you this to make it clear that I'm not approaching Perfect Blue from a feminist angle. My view is that all of life, from the smallest bacterium to the blue whale, is an abattoir where the strong feast upon the weak. While fossil fuels allowed us a brief reprieve from Malthusian brutality for a short few centuries, our population has increased, our technology has stagnated, and our climate is changing to the point that the "law of the jungle" is once again taking hold. I view Perfect Blue as a chronicle of the return of Japanese civilization (and all civilization more broadly) to something more primal as humanity leaves our peak years behind us. My expectation is that humans in 2200 will envy the lifestyles of peasants in 1200. Mima is a pop idol trying to transition into becoming an actress. As an idol, she mostly performed for horny middle-aged men and local louts, and she hopes for a more dignified career as she ages. Ironically, her background and the changing times get her cast in "degrading" roles, and her breakout role is playing a stripper who gets raped by the crowd. (Don't mind that scribbling you hear in the background, I'm just taking notes for my own work.) She also strips for various photoshoots (to my pleasure, said shots show her vulva - director Satoshi Kon doesn't pussy out in the way Western directors would). Throughout the film, we're treated to various shots showing murders and such, only to then hear a director yelling "Cut!" and realize that it was just shots from her acting career. So when actors and directors associated with Mima start turning up dead and an ugly stalker obsessed with Mima arrives without any cameras around, we start to realize that Mima is in actual danger. Figuring out what's real and what isn't is most of the fun of the film's incredible plotting, and while I personally didn't like the happy ending and twist culprit (I think it would have been more interesting to see Mima raped and killed by a deranged stalker, frankly), I understand that normal audiences would not be okay with that, and poor Mr. Kon probably wouldn't be invited to direct more high-budget films. My personal ending is that the film fades to black as the stalker assaults Mima. I watched Perfect Blue in the theater on a lark when I happened to come across its listing on Fandango (I watched Paprika by Kon years ago and was not impressed, so it's unlikely I would have watched this on my own without the prod from the theater). I'm utterly thrilled with Cinemark for airing all these re-releases and remasters (there's a remaster of classic anime Angel's Egg later this year that I also can't wait to catch). Most new films are frankly trash (they're all remakes or sequels because our present reality is so shitty that there's no source material to make movies about). But there's happily enough great movies from civilization's peak that we could just air them all in a loop and have more than enough to satisfy a human lifetime.

texto: 20th Century Studios 1.66:1 Colour + Monochrome 16mm + 35mm 18 “I must go punch that baby” Women in Film [2026] Poor Things is a tough watch in multiple ways, from its content and pacing to its arcs and themes. Granted, the standouts of its cast namely Emma Stone and its fabulous production design are nothing short of top tier. The fantastical world-building looks extraordinary on screen, and the former is intoxicating and engaging to watch, especially as it explores the comedic, albeit bizarre, context of the story. However, while Yorgos Lanthimos is evidently keen on exploring form both in space and in character, this experiment can only go on for so long without it becoming both tedious and somewhat excruciating to observe. For almost one hundred and fifty minutes this pushes the viewer to the maximum of concentration and comfort (difficult context aside) to sit with debilitating pacing that feels almost punishing to the viewer.

texto: A imagem que o filme tenta passar é muito boa ou isso é apenas o que as pessoas acreditam? Para mim, o filme fala sobre a autodescoberta da Bella como mulher e como pessoa. Além da autodescoberta, fala sobre o descobrimento do mundo na visão da propria. No inicio, o filme é acelerado. Ela cresce rapidamente, descobre tudo rapidamente. O filme em si tem acontecimentos atrás de acontecimentos e eu acredito que tudo isso esteja ligado à vontade de viver e explorar o mundo dela. Ao decorrer/final do filme, fica tudo muito arrastado. O filme tem 2h22 minutos, mas parece ter 5 horas, como se não tivesse fim. E para mim isso é conectado como a Bella tem se sentido. Não existe mais vontade de conhecer, explorar, descobrir as coisas da vida.  Ela apenas existe pois seu coração ainda bate, ela se arrasta. Apesar de tudo, é muito irônico que um filme que envolve tanta politica e gera a interpretação da liberdade feminina seja principalmente ligado ao sexo. O mais longe que uma mulher pode ir é virar uma prostituta em Paris ? O mais longe possível do auto descobrimento é se envolver com vários homens? Depois que ela cansou dessa vida, ela volta para aquilo que a propria chama de prisao. Ironico, nao?

texto: When people say Yorgos is just evil Wes Anderson…this is the movie they are hundred percent talking about. I came in very unsure what I would think of this one. Everybody I talked to either absolutely fucking loved it or fucking hated it. I’m kind of in a middle space with it. Undeniably visually beautifully. texto: • I enjoyed this movie well enough, although it leaned really hard into its quirkiness: the cartoonish sets, the cacophonic music, the embellished costumes, the overuse of fisheye lens • On its face, the movie is making a simple feminist argument. Bella is a blank slate adult, so she would seem to represent a woman if she could think, say, and do what she naturally wanted, without the influence of society. But under the surface, it’s not a straightforward feminist message (much like Barbie!). Yes she loves sex, but only with successful men (or once, with a tender woman). She finds the love of a kind, unthreatening man, and not once but twice runs away with a more powerful one who is certain to hurt her. She is created and taken advantage of by men with ethical and moral failings, but when she takes control of her own life, she follows the same path as Godwin and promptly oversees a similar surgical procedure.

texto: Feminism written through the highly sexualised visual perspective of men. A woman is so often associated with the consumption of her body whenever a film tries to portray female liberation, as if a woman’s freedom can only be expressed through her body. Bella was able to free herself from society’s expectations, yet the film framed that freedom through the very thing she should be liberated from.

texto: I really don’t know how to feel about this. The aesthetics are amazing and the idea is interesting, but there are things I just can’t ignore that make my experience watching this not as great as I would like. I can’t accept or pretend it’s normal for a grown man in his 30s to be lusting after and romantically captivated by a child in a woman’s body. To me, in all the sexual scenes, I couldn’t see anything more than men having sex with a child who doesn’t even understand what she’s doing and calls it “furious jumping.” She doesn’t have any actual idea about what’s happening and is driven by curiosity and the desire to satisfy the sexual urges that come with the body she’s now in. But that, to me, is still nothing more than a curious child trying to obtain “happiness,” as she calls it, through physical pleasure that she would otherwise have no understanding of if she hadn’t been placed in that woman’s adult body. Let’s not pretend that putting a feminist, female liberation framing around it makes something deeply disturbing any less disturbing than what it is: the sexualization of a character who is mentally a child, regardless of the fact that her body is that of an adult. All the amazing aesthetics and other praiseworthy visual aspects aside, this just ends up feeling like a poor representation of feminism through the eyes of a man. To me, if this was an attempt to make a statement and address the sexualization of children in today’s day and age, it failed miserably, because it ends up feeling more like a fantasy that normalizes the very things it tries to address.

texto: The art department absolutely ATE. Costumes, set design, make-up & sfx artists, visual direction…10/10 across the board, pure craftsmanship. As for the concept & screenplay? 2/10 A completely wasted opportunity. People keep calling this "subversive feminism," but the film’s actual structure tells a very different story. For over 80% of the runtime, we are forced to watch the voyeuristic objectification of a woman with the cognitive capacity of a child, left at the mercy of repulsive, predatory men. Calling this a 'journey toward sexual freedom' feels completely disingenuous when most of the movie is just a front-row seat to predatory men manipulating and mocking a woman's lack of boundaries. The supposed "subversion" is barely given any room to breathe. Bella’s actual intellectual, philosophical, and political awakening is crammed into the final act, acting as a thin, theoretical excuse to justify two hours of hyper-sexualization. There is a fine line between satirizing misogynistic reality and merely staging it for stylized entertainment, and the film crosses it completely. Stripped to its core, the movie spends nearly its entire duration packaging a deeply disturbing ethical conflict into a glossy visual spectacle. Wrapping predatory dynamic  in stunning aesthetics and calling it "liberation and empowerment " isn't subversive—it’s just intellectual laziness.

texto: I really don’t know how to feel about this. The aesthetics are amazing and the idea is interesting, but there are things I just can’t ignore that make my experience watching this not as great as I would like. I can’t accept or pretend it’s normal for a grown man in his 30s to be lusting after and romantically captivated by a child in a woman’s body. To me, in all the sexual scenes, I couldn’t see anything more than men having sex with a child who doesn’t even understand what she’s doing and calls it “furious jumping.” She doesn’t have any actual idea about what’s happening and is driven by curiosity and the desire to satisfy the sexual urges that come with the body she’s now in. But that, to me, is still nothing more than a curious child trying to obtain “happiness,” as she calls it, through physical pleasure that she would otherwise have no understanding of if she hadn’t been placed in that woman’s adult body. Let’s not pretend that putting a feminist, female liberation framing around it makes something deeply disturbing any less disturbing than what it is: the sexualization of a character who is mentally a child, regardless of the fact that her body is that of an adult. All the amazing aesthetics and other praiseworthy visual aspects aside, this just ends up feeling like a poor representation of feminism through the eyes of a man. To me, if this was an attempt to make a statement and address the sexualization of children in today’s day and age, it failed miserably, because it ends up feeling more like a fantasy that normalizes the very things it tries to address.

texto: The art department absolutely ATE. Costumes, set design, make-up & sfx artists, visual direction…10/10 across the board, pure craftsmanship. As for the concept & screenplay? 2/10 A completely wasted opportunity. People keep calling this "subversive feminism," but the film’s actual structure tells a very different story. For over 80% of the runtime, we are forced to watch the voyeuristic objectification of a woman with the cognitive capacity of a child, left at the mercy of repulsive, predatory men. Calling this a 'journey toward sexual freedom' feels completely disingenuous when most of the movie is just a front-row seat to predatory men manipulating and mocking a woman's lack of boundaries. The supposed "subversion" is barely given any room to breathe. Bella’s actual intellectual, philosophical, and political awakening is crammed into the final act, acting as a thin, theoretical excuse to justify two hours of hyper-sexualization. There is a fine line between satirizing misogynistic reality and merely staging it for stylized entertainment, and the film crosses it completely. Stripped to its core, the movie spends nearly its entire duration packaging a deeply disturbing ethical conflict into a glossy visual spectacle. Wrapping predatory dynamic  in stunning aesthetics and calling it "liberation and empowerment " isn't subversive—it’s just intellectual laziness.

exemplo: As reviews positivas destacam a atuação de Emma Stone como um dos pontos mais fortes do filme, com espectadores considerando-a uma das melhores da carreira e responsável por dar vida à personagem Bella, que se desenvolve de forma autêntica e marcante.
texto: Eu acho que não estava preparada para o quanto eu ia gostar de Pobres Criaturas. Comecei o filme sem saber direito o que esperar e terminei pensando em como uma história tão estranha conseguiu falar de coisas tão reais. Com certeza virou um dos meus filmes favoritos. A Bella é uma personagem muito diferente. No começo, ela está literalmente descobrindo o mundo, mas quanto mais ela conhece, mais começa a questionar tudo ao seu redor. E é justamente aí que o filme fica muito interessante: Bella não aceita que outras pessoas decidam o que ela pode ou não fazer. Pra mim, uma das maiores críticas do filme é justamente sobre a liberdade das mulheres. Durante toda a história, homens tentam controlar Bella, dizer o que ela deve fazer, como deve se comportar e até o que ela deve sentir. Só que, conforme ela conhece o mundo, ela percebe que não precisa viver dentro dessas regras. Ela quer conhecer, experimentar, errar e escolher por si mesma. E gosto muito que o filme não transforme essa liberdade em algo perfeito ou bonito o tempo inteiro. Bella toma decisões que podem ser consideradas erradas, passa por situações desconfortáveis e descobre coisas difíceis, mas ainda assim são experiências que pertencem a ela. Pela primeira vez, ela está vivendo a própria vida, e não a vida que alguém escolheu por ela. A estética também é uma das coisas que mais me conquistaram. Tudo parece um sonho meio estranho: os cenários, as cores, as roupas e até os movimentos da câmera. É exagerado e bizarro, mas combina perfeitamente com a forma como Bella enxerga o mundo. E a Emma Stone está simplesmente perfeita. A atuação dela faz a evolução da Bella parecer muito natural, principalmente porque conseguimos perceber a personagem mudando aos poucos, sem ela perder aquela personalidade curiosa e completamente fora do padrão. No final, Pobres Criaturas acabou sendo um filme que eu não esperava amar tanto. É estranho, engraçado, desconfortável e bonito ao mesmo tempo, mas principalmente é uma história sobre uma mulher descobrindo que ela tem o direito de escolher o próprio caminho. Virou facilmente um dos meus filmes favoritos, e acho que é daqueles que ficam na cabeça muito depois dos créditos.

Pra mim, uma das maiores críticas do filme é justamente sobre a liberdade das mulheres. Durante toda a história, homens tentam controlar Bella, dizer o que ela deve fazer, como deve se comportar e até o que ela deve sentir. Só que, conforme ela conhece o mundo, ela percebe que não precisa viver dentro dessas regras. Ela quer conhecer, experimentar, errar e escolher por si mesma. E gosto muito que o filme não transforme essa liberdade em algo perfeito ou bonito o tempo inteiro. Bella toma decisões que podem ser consideradas erradas, passa por situações desconfortáveis e descobre coisas difíceis, mas ainda assim são experiências que pertencem a ela. Pela primeira vez, ela está vivendo a própria vida, e não a vida que alguém escolheu por ela. A estética também é uma das coisas que mais me conquistaram. Tudo parece um sonho meio estranho: os cenários, as cores, as roupas e até os movimentos da câmera. É exagerado e bizarro, mas combina perfeitamente com a forma como Bella enxerga o mundo. E a Emma Stone está simplesmente perfeita. A atuação dela faz a evolução da Bella parecer muito natural, principalmente porque conseguimos perceber a personagem mudando aos poucos, sem ela perder aquela personalidade curiosa e completamente fora do padrão. No final, Pobres Criaturas acabou sendo um filme que eu não esperava amar tanto. É estranho, engraçado, desconfortável e bonito ao mesmo tempo, mas principalmente é uma história sobre uma mulher descobrindo que ela tem o direito de escolher o próprio caminho. Virou facilmente um dos meus filmes favoritos, e acho que é daqueles que ficam na cabeça muito depois dos créditos.

texto: Poor Things: Slut-Shaming Happening Both Onscreen and Off When a film receives such high praise while simultaneously stirring up so much controversy, where exactly does the problem lie? Is it the film itself, the audience, or even society at large? The movie is saturated with explicit sex scenes—some have gone so far as to call it pornography, saying "male audiences are having the best time." Others have gone further, questioning whether the film is a faux-feminist work riddled with the male gaze (their reasoning being that both the screenwriter and director are men). Yes, the male gaze is indeed pervasive—but it comes from a portion of the audience's own male gaze, as well as from a strain of feminism so pedantic it engages in self-imposed moral policing. A feminism that stigmatizes sex and refuses to engage with it is, in truth, still thinking through a patriarchal lens. (1) Only "Sluts" Exist, Never "Man-Whores"? "The sexuality of a woman as private property is moral; the sexuality of a woman as a subject is immoral." This notion almost fundamentally encapsulates the logic behind most of the moral criticism surrounding this film. From a modern societal perspective, attaching moral constraints to sex is perfectly reasonable—the problem is that rather than applying such standards equally to everyone, patriarchy's stigmatization of sex is aimed specifically at women. So when audiences watch Bella on the big screen masturbating without an ounce of shame, having sex with various men, and actively choosing to become a prostitute, plenty of viewers conclude that Bella is a "slut." They see her becoming a sex worker as a form of self-objectification—even though Bella is far from ordinary, possessing none of society's ingrained moral constructs. She masturbates simply for pleasure; her sexual encounters with various men are entirely consensual—she is, as a subject, freely unleashing her desires. (Setting aside the question of whether unrestrained indulgence is justifiable, the key point here is subject versus object.) Yet audiences still insist on seeing her as an object, convinced that she has been reduced to a product whose purpose is to please men with sex. They believe that female sexual liberation is a form of self-deception, that in the end women are still being "taken advantage of" by men. So the film's abundant display of the female lead's sexual scenes actually carries no inherent sense of the gaze—it is simply presentation. Yet many female viewers feel uncomfortable with the sex scenes in the film, developing a sense that these scenes come from a male-gaze perspective. In reality, it's because they have preemptively placed themselves in the position of the object, the passive party—a mindset that presupposes oneself as the victim. So when they see the female lead's sex scenes, and it happens that the director is male, they begin to conspiracy-theorize that patriarchal forces are trying to reap benefits by encouraging female sexual liberation. They think the film is patriarchy's sugar-coated trap—but in truth, patriarchy's trap was already planted in their own minds long ago. It's worth noting that the rakish lawyer Duncan in the film proudly boasts about having slept with many women. No one morally condemns him for it. Offscreen, men are likewise never shamed for having extensive sexual experience—on the contrary, they're seen as "impressive." And yet this same Duncan still believes he has the right to criticize Bella as a slut. So it turns out only "sluts" exist—never "man-whores." (2) Enlightenment Through Prostitution? One of the film's most controversial plot points is Bella actively choosing to become a prostitute—and clearly maturing and growing through that experience. This has led many to crudely interpret it as the director suggesting that prostitution can foster a woman's intellectual growth. Admittedly, the film's chosen mode of expression is provocative, but this prostitution episode is more symbolic of what the world perceives as "depravity." "We must experience everything—not just the good, but depravity, fear, and sorrow too." This doesn't mean we all need to become sex workers; rather, it means that experiencing hardship does indeed open the door to a person's inner world of thought and spirit. Someone who has only ever experienced pleasant things is destined never to become a mature person capable of deep reflection. (3) Is the Film Advocating Sexual Liberation? What About Social Systems? So the film does explore desire, but its purpose is not to advocate unbridled indulgence. And desire comes in many forms—sex is merely one dimension of it. But undeniably, sex delivers the greatest visual impact, and shattering ingrained perceptions requires a certain degree of shock. Therefore, the film's abundance of sexual imagery is not trying to say that sexual liberation is the most important pillar of feminism, nor is it attempting to obscure other issues. It isn't even really a feminist film—one might sooner call it a libertarian film that takes a passing jab at patriarchy. Don't forget that Bella is an infant in a fully grown body, devoid of society's ingrained moral constructs, utterly loyal to her own instincts and desires. We can never become Bella. Rather, through the shock that Bella's behavior delivers to us, we become aware of how much society's concepts restrict our thinking—how they keep us trapped in perpetual cycles of self-moralizing and judging others. As a surreal film with absurdist themes, it is destined to be considered immoral by society's moral standards. Fixating on that point yields little of value. We don't need to—and cannot—become Bella, nor do we need to impose moral constraints on Bella or the film. But that doesn't stop me from intuitively finding something beautiful in Bella's purity. Ultimately, a film can never change society. When it tries to point out the absurdity of certain social rules, the public turns around and accuses it of being heretical. Perhaps it is destined to be something the masses cannot understand—poor things, pointing straight at you and me.

texto: Some issues with editing, some issues with screenplay, loved mostly everything else. Tentatively a 7, will probably go up to an 8 on rewatch. Absolutely brilliant art direction, I loved the set design and the costume design, and I didn't even mind the CGI which even when obvious helped add to the visual surrealism of this movie. The cinematography is insane, every single frame of this movie makes it obvious that there is cinematography involved, and the film uses a very motivated wide selection of lenses to achieve this. I loved the really unconventional score as well. Emma Stone's performance is one of the best I've ever seen and she totally deserved the Oscar, Willem Dafoe is amazing as well (and the prosthetic make-up looks amazing), and I was shocked by how much I enjoyed Mark Ruffalo. Unfortunately I found this movie's commentary on womanhood and on wider society to be really shallow; far from offensive as others seem to find it, but not enough to drive the plot as long as it does. The movie is visually creative and entertaining enough to survive the long runtime anyway, but the screenplay struggles especially in the middle section. And while the editing mostly worked well on the small scale, it completely failed to communicate passage of time and left me very confused by the timeline of this film

texto: I need to offer something to the world and yet I have nothing. Comprendo la controversia con respecto a los temas que trata esta película. Es cierto que al menos al principio me chocó, pero creo que por describir ciertas situaciones no las está romantizando, justificando ni glorificando, sino incluso todo lo contrario. Durante toda la película Bella está en una constante guerra con lo que los hombres y la sociedad esperan de ella, intentando ser controlada de todas las formas posibles "recién nacida" en un mundo que no entiende. Que encontrase liberación personal de determinada manera no quita que esa vía que toma sea en sí misma un modo de explotación, y es más, hay un comentario que cuestiona esto en una escena. Sinceramente me la imaginaba mucho peor en este aspecto por lo que la gente comentaba, pero en mi opinión se tratan todos estos temas con precaución y astucia al mismo tiempo, sin que en ningún momento Bella pierda su autonomía ni su personalidad. A mí me ha flipado. Harry: Why do you stay with him? Bella: I always think it will be better. Brillante. Los juegos de cámara, las perspectivas, los escenarios y los vestuarios... Preciosos. Crea una atmósfera única. Trata muchísimas cuestiones muy diferentes (las injusticias, la naturaleza humana, las expectativas sociales, el matrimonio...) de manera interesante e ingeniosa. Papelón de Emma Stone. Aspiro a ser tan insoportable y despreocupada como Bella Baxter. I look at you and feel nothing but the lingering question: how did I ever want you?

texto: Foi muito interessante acompanhar o amadurecimento de Bella ao longo da trama, principalmente no trecho do navio, em que ela se dá conta da existência da pobreza e de como a sociedade pode ser mesquinha e cruel com os mais pobres. Porém, a tentativa de tratar a sexualidade como a ferramenta central de libertação feminina acaba se perdendo ao longo da obra. Especialmente na fase em Paris, com a entrada na prostituição, o filme exagera na quantidade de cenas explícitas. O problema não é a presença do sexo na tela em si, mas sim a sua repetição exaustiva. Em vez de continuar desenvolvendo a mente e o intelecto em expansão de Bella, explorando sua forma única de descobrir o mundo, de construir afetos e de se relacionar com as pessoas, a direção prefere dar voltas no mesmo choque visual. Como dirigida por um homem, a experiência passa inevitavelmente pelo filtro do olhar masculino. Fica a nítida impressão de que a direção reduziu a "liberdade da mulher" a uma visão puramente corporal, esquecendo-se de que a descoberta de Bella já tinha ido muito além da sexualidade.
