texto: Llevar una de las comedias más influyentes de la historia de la televisión a la gran pantalla era una maniobra inevitable, pero cargada de riesgos. Estrenada tras años de especulaciones y en un punto donde la serie de televisión ya mostraba signos claros de desgaste creativo, Los Simpson: La película asumió el reto de transformar una dinámica televisiva de 22 minutos en un evento cinematográfico de escala global. El resultado es un largometraje sumamente entretenido, vistoso y con picos cómicos altísimos, aunque empañado por decisiones narrativas que se alejan de la esencia más pura de Springfield. El apartado visual es, sin lugar a dudas, uno de sus puntos más sólidos. La transición hacia un dibujo más estilizado, apoyado por sombreados digitales y una paleta de colores vibrante, le otorgó al largometraje la escala de evento que exigía el cine. La dirección aprovecha las dimensiones de la pantalla grande para desplegar secuencias mucho más dinámicas —como la construcción de la cúpula sobre Springfield o el escape de la familia—, respaldadas por una banda sonora de John Powell que eleva la tensión sin perder la ironía característica de la franquicia. Sin embargo, el núcleo de la historia tropieza en la definición de sus prioridades. El conflicto central opta por apoyarse de forma casi exclusiva en una crisis matrimonial entre Homero y Marge, una fórmula narrativa ampliamente explotada en la serie que aquí se percibe cargada de clichés románticos. La decisión de volcar la carga emotiva en el reencuentro de la pareja le resta espacio al desarrollo de otras dinámicas de la ciudad y fuerza un todo sentimental que por momentos se siente ajeno a la acidez satírica que convirtió a la serie en un fenómeno cultural. A esto se suma una caracterización de Homero que no termina de asentarse. Si bien cuenta con momentos memorables dentro del metraje, se extrañan aquellos rasgos de su personalidad que construyeron sus mejores épocas en televisión: esa mezcla única entre tontería entrañable, momentos de astucia involuntaria y una relación más auténtica con sus vecinos y su entorno. En la película, gran parte de sus acciones quedan subordinadas a empujar el conflicto romántico, dejando en segundo plano su faceta como catalizador del caos social de Springfield. Los Simpson: La película funciona muy bien como pieza de entretenimiento rápido y cumple con el cometido de reunir a generaciones frente a la pantalla. Posee un ritmo ágil y chistes que han quedado grabados en la cultura popular, pero al balancear los elementos, queda la sensación de que prefirió ir a lo seguro antes que arriesgarse a construir un relato verdaderamente memorable. Un hito visual y nostálgico que aprueba con solvencia, pero que se queda lejos del brillo de los mejores años de la familia amarilla. Una entrega entretenida y técnicamente impecable que cumple con el espectáculo visual que exige la gran pantalla. Sin embargo, su dependencia de un conflicto romántico trillado y la pérdida de matices clave en Homero le impiden alcanzar el nivel de los mejores capítulos de la serie.

texto: Having premiered nearly forty years ago, The Simpsons is one of the longest last series airing on television.  However you may feel about its quality as it progresses, it is a testament to how popular it is that it has lasted as long as it has.  Of course, given said popularity, it was inevitable that movie starring the residents of Springfield would come to fruition.  When it comes to series being adapted to film, The Simpsons Movie is not among the worst of its kind and is entertaining.  However, it does come with a few of its own drawbacks. The Simpsons Movie goes for a grander plotline that is more fitting for a ninety minute feature than a half hour special.  This time, it is a series of careless accidents brought upon by Homer Simpson that brings great danger to Springfield.  Homer has been known for getting into trouble because of his stupidity or outright selfishness but it's a whole town that's at stake because of his flaws as opposed to matters with family or close friends.  It is a plot that does fit in with what the series was about, even having some clever political jokes here and there. Where the film does suffer a little is that, even with the more epic storyline, it also feels like an extended episode of the show.  This might hit a little differently for people who watch the show religiously while newcomers may be confused.  There are a few laughs to be found from fourth wall jokes and innuendos (some of which would have been censored on the actual show) but it also feels like it's fan service.  It's especially evident when random recurring characters pop up to do what the audience expects without really contributing too much to the actual plot.  Furthermore, the moments that are meant to feel emotional feel a little too quick to make way for some more jokes and action set pieces. The animation of the film keeps true to that of the show along with Matt Groening's own style.  It has been clearly been upgraded for a cinematic outing as it adds more shading and color, reflecting the higher budget.  At times it is even more fluid, partially a result of some former Disney animators having a hand in the making of it (There are a couple of humorous jokes at their expense as well).  It's a style that may not appeal to everyone, but fans of the show should be pleased that it doesn't go for something completely different on a technical level. All the original cast members return to voice their respective characters.  Dan Castellaneta does manage to capture Homer's dimwitted nature.  It is a little hard to get behind the character at times due to how emotionally distant he is for much of the film but Castellaneta is still having fun.  Julie Kavner gets more of a chance to show some range as Marge Simpson.  Bart feels a bit more short changed as he does have a potentially compelling plot but it's not given enough development though Nancy Cartwright still brings her A-game.  Albert Brooks is entertaining as a newcomer, the villainous Russ Cargill, who takes advantage of Homer's accidents in order to destroy Springfield. The Simpsons Movie is a mostly humorous, if slight adaptation of the series.  Much of the time it does feel like it is pandering to fans or stretching out a story way too thin.  Still, its entertainment value lies on its production, the voice acting and some clever writing and jokes.  It is one of the more decent theatrical adaptations of an animated TV show.

texto: O mueres siendo la mejor comedia animada de la historia o vives lo suficiente para hacer una parodia de ti mismo. La película de los Simpson es bastante polarizante para mí. Salió en una época donde la serie ya estaba en declive y llevaba un par de años sin las voces originales en latino. Es inevitable compararla con los años dorados de la serie y ahí es cuando la película se siente sin esa gran carisma de las primeras 10 temporadas. Incluso en su fecha de estreno no me terminó de convencer, la comedia había perdido algo de chispa y las caracterizaciones de los personajes eran cada vez más planas. Homero en esta película es insufrible, cruel, extremadamente irresponsable y bobo. Lejos de ese padre torpe pero amoroso que solía ser. Tendrá su arco de redención al final, que al menos medio funciona. La serie se caracteriza por sus variadas estrellas invitadas y aquí me agrada la aparición de Green Day. La trama del domo y la destrucción de Springfield está ok. Los Simpson significan mucho para mí, marcaron mi infancia. Quisiera darle mejor calificación por mi amor a la serie, pero prefiero poner la temporada 6 en DVD que ver esta peli de nuevo.

texto: This was a childhood favorite for me so it was kind of a hard watch looking past the rose-tinted glasses as not only an older viewer, but also as someone who does still deeply love classic Simpsons. The jokes that I remember still hit today, but a lot were trying to land off the idea of finding Homer’s horrible personality in this movie to be funny. It just wasn’t. In the way that The Spongebob Movie is often referred to as the last piece of good classic Spongebob, I feel The Simpsons Movie is a weird science experiment of classic Simpsons and modern Simpsons comedy that blends together in a strange new form that doesn’t work for me as it once did as a child who just saw “The Funny Yellow Family”. There are remnants of what made The Simpsons so good for me even today here. Theres pieces of genuine heartfelt moments that you’d find in the golden era, but you have to trudge through the off characterization and unfunny jokes that Homer is just the worst but will eventually be forgiven because he’s the main man. I don’t like it, it feels bad.

texto: This movie is the last dieing breath of what once was a great television show, ran into the ground from the greedy company’s that be. From the start Homer Simpson and the rest of the Simpsons crews antics are unenjoyable and outlandish. The show was made great from the grounded premise and storylines, they make Homer (Simpson) and unlikable jerk who’s crimes arnt just against the city of Springfield but to the rest of his family aswell (the Simpsons). His lovable juvenile character from early seasons is dumbed down to that of an knit-witted moron whose actions range from stupid to down right evil, poisoning the towns water supply and fleeing to Alaska. If I was Marge (Simpson) I would have left that yellow glutton long ago. The rest of the cast isn’t much better with Bart being naked on my tv not being very funny, actually quite the opposite. The saving grace is the animation and visuals which still not amazing are definitely a step up from the show.

texto: The movie manages to preserve the spirit of the series, with its irreverent humor, social and political satire, and that wonderfully absurd quality that has made the Simpson family a pop-culture icon. Homer is, naturally, at the heart of it all, and his perfect combination of stupidity, selfishness, and genuine love for his family still works brilliantly. It may not offer anything particularly groundbreaking compared to the series, and because it stays so faithful to its original style, at times it feels like watching a very long episode. But that's also its greatest strength: it never tries to become something The Simpsons isn't. Funny, irreverent, and packed with memorable moments. It may not be the deepest or most innovative animated movie out there, but for a Simpsons fan, it's almost impossible not to have a great time watching it.

texto: I think one of the reasons this works so well for me is the timelessness of the comedy, you could put this movie in theaters today and change nothing and it'd still be a hit, something that can't be said for many many comedies. Besides aging wonderfully comedically, the story here is exactly what I personally love for theatrical TV movies. There's a plot that warrants a longer runtime yet still space for small bits and antics that make it feel like I'm still watching an episode. This might sound insane but I really cannot stand it when a TV show gets a theatrical release and it feels like I'm watching TV characters in a movie not  a longer higher budget episode. Examples of ones I like are this obviously, the Bob's Burgers movie, Mask of the Phantasm, Cowboy Bebop and ofc like the Demon Slayer, JJK, AOT movies, versus things like the Fullmetal Alchemist movies that feel like transplanted characters in a plot and lowkey detracts from the overall narrative. Anyways off that tangent I really really wish they stuck with emotional beat of Marge leaving Homer a little bit longer, because as thousands of people have said that's by far the strongest moment of the whole film. The animation was something I appreciated as well, swinging the camera around and using perspective in ways you don't see in episodes. All around I had a great time, I'm sad I got banned from watching the Simpsons and didn't get to watch this growing up

Maybe I'll come back to it someday.

Examples of ones I like are this obviously, the Bob's Burgers movie, Mask of the Phantasm, Cowboy Bebop and ofc like the Demon Slayer, JJK, AOT movies, versus things like the Fullmetal Alchemist movies that feel like transplanted characters in a plot and lowkey detracts from the overall narrative. Anyways off that tangent I really really wish they stuck with emotional beat of Marge leaving Homer a little bit longer, because as thousands of people have said that's by far the strongest moment of the whole film. The animation was something I appreciated as well, swinging the camera around and using perspective in ways you don't see in episodes. All around I had a great time, I'm sad I got banned from watching the Simpsons and didn't get to watch this growing up

texto: While on the surface, this film feels like a continuation of the extremely long running beloved animated series, it really is a deeply complex insight into the world of a (almost) nuclear family on the brink of destruction due to an emotionally absent father. When considering that this movie came out in 2007 at the height of the 5th Harry Potter film, Spider-Man 3, and the newest Pirates of the Caribbean, this movie, often flies under the radar for being one of the most insightful movies of the year. However, this doesn’t mean that its impact is any less important. While, it didn’t break any records in the box office it’s still manages to give an extremely nuanced view at the detriment behind what will occur when somebody chooses themselves over their loved ones. Homer in this showcases his duality by stepping into the antagonist role by being a character that just can’t seems to stop screwing up. As a result of this, he ends up, turning his entire family and friends against him and as audience members we get to watch him deal with the isolation involved with destroying the structured comfortability associated with familial ties. This is an extremely refreshing take on the series since often cheap jokes are written off to excuse Homer for his genuinely awful behavior. This movie does something smart by allowing the audience to see how Homer’s actions towards his family create turmoil to the point of Marge literally stealing the kids to take them away from the situation Homer has caused. This film is not only a masterclass in the human condition, but it also showcases how regardless of how terrible of a person homer is he still like every human deserves forgiveness. It’s sort of a beautiful story wrapped up in a 90 minute runtime that had me laughing as hard as I did the first time I watched it. Also, it has spider pig and he’s awesome.

texto: A remarkably boring sequel only remembered for its last 15 minutes. Story is a stunning departure from the creativity, wit, and intelligence of the first two films, with its never-funny script, downgraded character writing, and predictable narrative. Opening sequence and many other story details are notably derivative as lame nostalgia-copies of earlier material. As with most in Pixar's 2000s output, film's animation is flat and generic. texto: 11 years on from Toy Story 2, the trilogy was completed with an epic prison escape movie written to close out the franchise. Toy Story 3 is a film I’m very conflicted on, because in fleeting moments I catch the brilliance the high letterboxd score would suggest and the third act is (mostly) as good as they say. The ending is enough to make any grown man sniffle, it would have been a great place to leave the franchise if it didn’t ultimately continue. But I have serious gripes with the film I can’t ignore, that frankly leave it well short of the first two films in the Toy Story trilogy turned pentalogy Firstly a brief note on the creation process. Toy Story 3 began life in 2004, remaining at the tentative stage due to the complications of the Disney deal I touch on in my Toy Story 1 and 2 reviews. Eventually Disney bought out the company, and work was restarted on Toy Story 3 with a new script and an absurd $200 million budget. That is over twice the budget of Toy Story 2 which I remind you was scrapped and restarted entirely. In 2010 the movie finally released to much critical and commercial success, becoming the fourth highest grossing film of all time (now barely in the top 50, inflation is a funny thing) and featuring on multiple top 10 films of the 2010s lists The film mostly moves away from the A plot B plot structure of the first two films and instead has the gang almost entirely together. Woody has a short stint away from the Daycare, outside of that we stick with the entire cast of toys the whole way through. Getting some big problems out the way early, the cast here is not even half as good as they were in Toy Story 2. Mr Potato Head is a shell of his former self, Ham might as well be an extra, Slinky has been neutered to having no jokes at all, Jessie has much less bite than her debut appearance. I laughed maybe twice, three times the entire film. Meanwhile Toy Story 2 had me in stitches the whole way through. The biggest casualty is Buzz, who they so clearly have no fucking idea what to do with so they do a ‘Buzz is back to his default setting’ story AGAIN. In all three of the original Toy Story trilogy we have Buzz thinking he’s not a toy, that’s absolutely egregious. The second justifies it with it being a seperate Buzz and the comedy being on point, here he’s placed in an antagonist role and it’s ass. Speaking of ass and antagonists, Lotso fucking sucks. It’s just stinky Pete but again! It’s the exact same villain but worse in every conceivable way. One of Disney’s worst villains, a complete charisma vacuum who is half baked and poorly written The themes of Toy Story 3 are around growing up, moving on, accepting that things change and making peace with that. At least, that’s what the final act would suggest. But unlike the first two films which did a brilliant job to make the plot contribute to the greater themes being explored, Toy Story 3 forces it’s ideas into the first and last 15 minutes with absolutely nothing in-between. So for a good amount of the run time, it really is just ‘woody was right the whole time 😱’ which we’ve done already and a prison escape movie. Alas, it’s not even a very good prison escape movie with the escape sequence being undercooked and not on par with the first two films action sequences. Toy Story 1 and 2 are not only funnier but more dramatically intense, Toy Story 3 uses middling jokes as a crutch for a lack of interesting stakes because again the villain is pathetic and the personal stakes for anyone other than Woody feel minuscule Yes the last stretch is great. The imagery of the incinerator rules, although the aliens saving them with the giant claw borders on Dues Ex Machina in its absurdity and somewhat undercuts the whole melting alive thing. The scene where Andy plays with the toys with Bonnie is beautiful. Woody saying ‘so long, partner’ and realising he belongs with the other Toy’s and not at College is great. I just wish these moments felt more earned, I don’t think much of anything in the second act resonates with the resolution thematically or even tonally Toy Story 3 is a misfire in the franchise for mine. It doesn’t have anywhere close to the meticulous plotting or comedic timing of the first two films, and is for mine a step below in just about every way. This includes animation by the way, the Toys move far more cartoonish with looney toons physics which takes away a huge part of the charm of the original two films. The toys actually moved like toys, in the third instalment they don’t. It’s the attention to detail that really derails the end of the trilogy for mine, and is probably why I didn’t have a visceral reaction to a fourth or fifth or sixth that others have had. I’d even argue that while Toy Story 3 has a nice ending it doesn’t wrap up the entire franchise in this perfect bow that should never have been touched. It’s the end of Andy’s story but Woody and especially Buzz don’t get anything close to satisfying conclusions to their journeys. And yet in the Andy farewell movie we spend almost all of it away from Andy… again! Wouldn’t it have made way more sense to spend more time with Andy and actually explore that relationship beyond a sense of duty. Explore the emotional dilemma Woody faces, loyalty to his best friend or acceptance that his friend grows up in a way he won’t. And how Buzz relates to that, drawing back to the first film in which Woody reacts to potential replacement with resentment and jealousy. We can see how Woody’s character has evolved through his connection to Buzz and with age. As is, this isn’t even close to the perfect farewell film people insinuate it is

texto: What made the first two Toy Story films work so well was the sense of deeper characterisation and internal conflict that formed an emotional backbone for the toys’ colourful adventures; Woody learning to accept Buzz in the first film or weighing the decision to become a museum piece in the second both served as the kind of substantial character arc that is conspicuously absent from the third, which here reduces him to a righteous Cassandra figure trying to rescue his friends from daycare well before its hidden darkness is revealed (a saviour complex that the fourth film correctly chooses to deconstruct in order to properly close the loop on him as a character). In trying to give the toys what was presumably going to be one last adventure, it sacrifices that particular sense of character for the sake of a perfunctory prison-break parody and a handful of precisely-calibrated emotional moments around which the entire film seems to have been reverse-engineered. The recent sequels had their flaws, but they still understood the need to give these toys some semblance of interiority that could be challenged by more than just the excitement and thrills posed by external obstacles - as a result, the inclusion of a Totoro doll seem less like one iconic studio tipping its cap to another than it does an ironic reminder of how far removed Pixar could get from Ghibli’s nuanced approach to animation.

It’s a sort of bittersweet look at what if feels like to grow up and let go.

texto: “Authority should be derived from the consent of the governed, not from the threat of force.” - Barbie. Change is terrifying - to have to confront the idea of your comfort being threatened, something you’ve known and experienced being replaced with something new and frightening, it takes a lot to overcome it. The Toy Story series have been a lot of things - it’s been more than 30 years since the first one revolutionised animation and thy just released a new one, the fifth in a long line of critically and commercially acclaimed films, but none of them are as good as Toy Story 3; its not just about sentient plastic, but about love, growth, comfort, purpose, betrayal and the idea of moving on, and it’s constructed in a manner that is inexplicably beautiful because of its masterful script and direction. Out of the three films so far in the series (and from the ones that came after), Toy Story 3 is the most emotionally mature, mainly because of how well it deals with the aforementioned themes - in a manner that is not just easy for a child to understand, but also for an adult who grew up with these films to appreciate and love. What starts as a standard lost and found story that has become the standard operating procedure for these films quickly evolves into a full blown “heist-like” feature, supplemented with some of the most heart-rending sub plots you could find in a film that is supposed to be marketed towards children. The tonal consistency in the screenplay is astounding, because this film manages to be so many things without trying too hard to be - it’s sad, funny (cackling and giggling funny), intelligent and down-right moving. The film also draws strength from the fact that it holds one of the most outrageously well written villains I could imagine. Lotso is literally Dr Doom levels of machiavellian evil, and it’s shockingly good! This is a character who’s heart was torn apart and is so full of pain and resentment that he refuses to accept any kind of attempt at redemption, right until the very end - it’s all done so well that you fully understand why he is the way he is, but never sympathise or justify his actions because of how cruel he is. It’s fucking brilliant I tell you, way too brilliant for a children’s movie. At its core, Toy Story 3 is about change, and how some people are able to cope with it, and how some aren’t. There’s a reason this is called one of the greatest animated films of all time, and it’s a title that is truly warranted.

texto: Toy Story 3 is a great conclusion to Toy Story series, you’ll see what I mean when I talk about the fourth film. Looking through the movie, the first thing is that this is mostly a prison break film, which is certainly a unique option but it’s done very well with the style change. The animation has gotten to a point where it is equivalent to real life, especially with all the grime the toys get and the incinerator with millions of moving trash pieces by physics. The characters are very good, with all the original cast returning, expect for Bo, who would have broke into a million pieces during most of this film. The new characters are just as good, we get Lotso, possibly the best of an original animated villain by Pixar besides Syndrome, then an specific Barbie and Ken, probably the best at teaching me about the Barbie line without watching all 37 animated movies by Mattel, Ken is voiced by Micheal Caine, so he’s a British Ken. Then for all of Bonnie’s toys, they all done well in the film, some interesting casting is Trixie being Mabel from Gravity Falls, and Mr. Pricklepants being voiced by the late-80s Bond, Dalton. I personally think the best part though is Andy throughout the film. I, myself, am growing up, and I can relate to Andy aging and giving his toys away to a new generation. The ending still does make me cry to this day, and that is telling on how impactful this movie is. If there is a series that should all get 5 stars together, I'll say this one may be a contender. I guess the only bad thing is that Disney bought the rights to the cymbal monkey toy and, even though they never use it ever besides this film, they will file a lawsuit against any film using the monkey toy like The Monkey. I guess this is what happens when Disney is a capitalist company owning a product line patent.

texto: Tldr this would go so hard if I was 6 years old When Rachel told me tonight's movie was going to be Michael Bay's Transformers , I was a bit trepidatious. It's a bit of a cultural blind spot for me - I knew a lot about the film, I'd seen a lot of clips of Shia LaBeouf from the films, but never actually watched or engaged with anything from the Transformers franchise. Suffice to say it, the cultural footprint is familiar, even if the film itself was not. Over a pre-film game of catch, as if to underline the upcoming vibes, we heard the distant roar of a Eurofighter Typhoon fighter jet, some miles away. That's not a regular occurrence in northwest London but today is apparent RAF day. Rachel was hyped, and she was hyping it up. We begin in a place that is absolutely Qatar. Why? Don't ask questions, enjoy the film. Things get messy real quick and I'll say this; this film looks fantastic. It is true what they say about CGI taking a step back since 2007. Maybe it's that there's just a lot going on or that the camera is always shaking: it doesn't matter, the decepticons, the autobots, and everything in between look probably exactly how you'd want them to look in a live-action film. Where were we? Ah yeah, havoc being wreaked on the US military industrial complex, getting steadily closer to home. Why is the little decepticon dude having an orgasm while he hacks? Freaky lil guy. Shia LaBeouf is easily the best part of this film, along with John Turturro. Genuinely funny, not necessarily served with the best writing, but gets an itchy energy that works really well for the film. I vaguely remember most of my school peers thirsting over Megan Fox in early secondary school. I get that, but her near-flawless conventional beauty doesn't make up for a total absence of acting talent. It becomes apparent that choices made by Michael Bay and the production team are designed to hide this with suggestive shots, and talk about engines that is never really truly about engines. This continues to a lesser extent as the film goes on. I worry these days that I'm too close to the action. I work semi-adjacently to defence, I play a lot of Arma, and I take an interest in geopolitics and defence policy. It's this knowledge that curses me, and forces me to sigh - yes, I know, it's a film about talking cars and vehicles from space - but if you're going to embrace the military industrial complex and essentially show off its power, you can't have A-10s go from dispatch to munitions delivery in 35 seconds (it's at least 35 minutes. At least ). The characterisation of some of these people is utterly diabolical, and almost certainly a product of the time. For example, there is 1 (one) black character who doesn't spend most lines of dialogue screaming/overreacting. Sam's parents must have been the inspiration for the Payday 3 security guards ("must have been the wind" ahhhh parents). But it's ok, the plot is shaky too. It's fine to begin with, but the plot holes come thick and fast, for example: - Sector 7 captures Sam and Mikaela and it's a big sad scene and everyone's angry at each other - it's the low point to end Act 2: but the next time we see them they're all chummy and gold and on a helicopter with the Secretary of Defence? Felt unearned. - We should keep Megatron under critical infrastructure, like the Hoover dam - President Hoover founded Sector 7, after all! - Wait, why has Secretary Voight gone with the hackers™ and John Turturro and hasn't got a platoon of security detail with him? He's the mf secretary of defence!!? - We need to get the allspice - sorry - the allspark away from here: let's go to a major population centre. Nothing bad has ever happened in a major population centre. - Every time Sam or Mikaela gets caught by one of the autobots after falling a height, that's gotta hurt so damn much - Wait, that's it? what did Sam actually do there? If Megatron wanted the allspice and all it took was that, why didn't he do that first?? - Ending scene: cuck car park None of this is to say I had a bad time though 🙂 It was great fun to watch a bit of a cornerstone of 2000s cinema and a part of many of my friends' personal canon. I wasn't there early enough, so I probably missed out - that's alright by me though.

texto: Enjoyable movie. Shia Labeouf did a great job. I think his fidgety, anxious but courageous character is one of my favorite parts about this movie. Bumblebee and Optimus have awesome “aura” moments where they just steal the spotlight. Megatron as a villain is very interesting. The movie was a fun watch. The transformers were supposed to save the day and be the protectors. While they did do that, I think they learned just as much as the audience that HUMANS are not just going to be pushed around. Shia’s character is the sole example of why Optimus is fighting to save Earth. He is teaching the auto bots there is more that meets the eye. Cons, I think at times it seemed very fast paced. There are some moments that were hard to keep up with. The first half of the movie was very lackluster, the second half picks up a bit I did like the comedic relief in that half but what helps define this movie is the final act. Also it is hard to tell some of the robots apart. The biggest downside in my opinion is the lack of character depth to a lot of the robots and humans. In conclusion, the movie is a good watch. I think the cgi looks great even for today’s time. However, I personally believe there is a spark missing that could have made it better. 3/5

texto: I grew up watching Transformers as a kid, and I was completely into it. I had all the little robot toys, and I can still remember having fun transforming them and playing with them while watching the cartoon. So when this movie came out, there was definitely a part of me that was excited to see these characters brought to the big screen. And honestly, Transformers delivers pretty well on that childhood nostalgia. Seeing Optimus Prime, Bumblebee, Megatron, Starscream and the rest of the Transformers brought to life with modern special effects was pretty damn cool. The designs and transformations felt like a natural evolution of what I remembered from the cartoon, and the movie actually captures a lot of the spirit of what made the original series fun. Watching these giant robots transform, fight and tear up the screen is exactly the kind of thing younger me would have loved. As an adult, though, I can also see the movie’s flaws. The story isn’t anything groundbreaking, some of the human characters and comedy don’t always work for me, and at times it feels more like a showcase for the special effects than a great story. But I never really expected Transformers to be some deep cinematic experience. I wanted to have fun with it, and that’s exactly what I got. The action is entertaining, the effects still hold up pretty well, and there’s something satisfying about seeing characters I grew up with finally getting the big-budget treatment. Is it the best movie I’ve ever seen? Definitely not. Is it a bad movie? Not at all. For me, Transformers is simply a fun, nostalgic ride that brought a piece of my childhood back to the big screen.

texto: Bon... Bah c'est d'la merde. Non, soyons sérieux : les effets visuels sont très réussis. Après, est-ce que ça suffit à en faire un bon film ? Spoiler : non. Le scénario est un pétard mouillé. Bon, ça c'est pas trop grave : je suis un des plus grands défenseurs de Pacific Rim, qui lui non plus ne brille pas par son scénario (quoique il maîtrise bien plus la caractérisation et le développement de ses personnages). Mais si en plus d'un scénario pourri digne des pires Emmerich, la mise en scène est pas ouf, bah ça devient vachement insipide. Et Michael Bay a beau faire plein de transformations de robots et une tonne d'explosion, ça ne fait ni chaud ni froid. Les personnages sont mal construits, la photo est laide, les couleurs sont délavées et m'ont rappelés Snyder (et ce n'est clairement pas un compliment), et en plus dans tout ça, Bay masque la médiocrité de sa mise en scène par des boum boum et des grosses voitures. Alors il y a quelques idées par-ci par-là, et certaines scènes d'action assez rigolotes, mais c'est jamais très impressionnant, jamais d'effet whaou, et dans un film qui pourtant n'a que ça pour briller, bah c'est très con. Ceci dit, et je conclurai là-dessus, c'est divertissant. Et ça je ne peux pas le reprocher à Michael Bay : c'est moche, c'est con, mais c'est rigolo.

texto: I wish I had a polarizing take on Transformers (2007), but as a product of the 2000s, this had little impact on my life at a time that it very well could have. Some Michael Bay enthusiasts I know are unapologetically in love with the Transformers franchise, and I'll admit that I see the appeal. This is a bombastic, explosive, ten-toes-down blockbuster with commentary about military, police, and humanity, and it looks pretty great while doing it... but similarly to some of the Americanized Godzilla films, while I had a good time with this one, it failed to leave much of a lasting impression on me. I will give the film credit for its action sequences; it's over-the-top and impressive in its blockbuster filmmaking, especially for 2007. The CGI holds up refreshingly well, and the cliches aren't executed haphazardly. I think part of the disconnect comes from a lack of literacy in Bay's filmography, which I plan to rectify sooner rather than later, but I also struggle to reconcile that with the lack of humanity in the human characters. I found the Transformers themselves infinitely more interesting than Sam, Mikaela, or any of the other human characters. Sure, that's somewhat to be expected in the Transformers movie, but this 144-minute action extravaganza spent enough time on the humans to give me more meaningful time with them or more depth to the Transformers. I suppose I can find more of that in the next three films. Ultimately, I think there's room for me to appreciate this more on rewatch, but this is good, not great to my tastes as of today.

texto: I grew up watching Transformers as a kid, and I was completely into it. I had all the little robot toys, and I can still remember having fun transforming them and playing with them while watching the cartoon. So when this movie came out, there was definitely a part of me that was excited to see these characters brought to the big screen. And honestly, Transformers delivers pretty well on that childhood nostalgia. Seeing Optimus Prime, Bumblebee, Megatron, Starscream and the rest of the Transformers brought to life with modern special effects was pretty damn cool. The designs and transformations felt like a natural evolution of what I remembered from the cartoon, and the movie actually captures a lot of the spirit of what made the original series fun. Watching these giant robots transform, fight and tear up the screen is exactly the kind of thing younger me would have loved. As an adult, though, I can also see the movie’s flaws. The story isn’t anything groundbreaking, some of the human characters and comedy don’t always work for me, and at times it feels more like a showcase for the special effects than a great story. But I never really expected Transformers to be some deep cinematic experience. I wanted to have fun with it, and that’s exactly what I got. The action is entertaining, the effects still hold up pretty well, and there’s something satisfying about seeing characters I grew up with finally getting the big-budget treatment. Is it the best movie I’ve ever seen? Definitely not. Is it a bad movie? Not at all. For me, Transformers is simply a fun, nostalgic ride that brought a piece of my childhood back to the big screen.

texto: 2.5/10 "The first Transformers is actually kinda good." That's a sentence I've heard loads of times. I have no idea what's going on in the minds of the people who say that. The first Transformers is one of the most embarrassing AAA productions I know of. And it only goes downhill from here. The entire movie's attitude is just loathsome. It tries to mash a few dark and serious elements together with dialogue and comic relief straight out of a frat house. Every character is unbelievably obnoxious. I don't understand why anyone would ever want to follow these people, or why anyone would ever care about anything that's happening. The entire world this film takes place in is insufferable, and the whole thing feels like it was made by a bunch of college jocks. Everything about it is just annoying. It's also weird how often the movie seems to be attempting some kind of parody of the American government. The directing is actually okay for a production like this. The blend of on-set footage and CGI works great, and Bay directs the actors competently. What I do find hilarious, however, is just how clearly his background in music video directing shines through in quite a few shots. That - and especially how aggressively everything is geared towards being cool and badass - comes off as incredibly cringe and try-hard. Ninety per cent of the story is made up of some lame McGuffin fetch quest with stakes I couldn't care less about, because the world and the characters suck. And it all eventually culminates in one of the least exciting third acts I've ever seen. There's battle scene after battle scene, but not only do I barely know what's going on because half the Transformers look the same, I also don't really care. It's just more and more fighting, and I realised that watching Transformers transform into and out of cars had already gotten boring the third time around. This film is filled to the brim with stupid shit and is, in general, one of the most unenjoyable ways to spend two hours and fifteen minutes that I can think of.

While the story between Sam (Shia LaBeouf) and Bumblebee (Mark Ryan) can be a grounding moment, it isn’t enough force to get it on land. Neither is Peter Cullen’s performance as Optimus Prime, the score, or the fights. Optimus owing his life to Sam does make sense though and Optimus says his iconic lines and good new lines. But that’s just about where the fun ends. First, Michael Bay doesn’t seem to respect the lore for Cybertron is supposed to be habitable, at least for the Decepticons. There’s too many subplots, the wrong tone with the military and disaster film aspects, too detailed CGI with the Decepticons being all gray, too much human stuff, bad jokes, especially Bumblebee and the lubricant and Ratchet (Robert Foxworth) saying Sam’s pheromone levels suggests he wants to have a kid with Mikaela (Megan Fox). Also the whole Sam selling his great-grandfather’s glasses on eBay is meaningless. Shia LaBeouf is just alright as Sam, he tries, but Bay, Roberto Orci, and Alex Kurtzman don’t give him much to work with. So little that Sam doesn’t feel like a hero as he’s given no space to grow into one. Megan Fox is also not impressive as she is subjected to Bay sexualizing her, even when doing something as simple as looking into what’s wrong with a car. Although that’s more so how she is dressed. Bay and Fox have history, as she was portrayed at 15 quite suggestively in Bad Boys II (2003), and Fox did not forget that. This movie doesn’t feel like a step in the right direction with Fox in Bay’s movies. Especially since she doesn’t have much of a character and is mostly here so Bay can feature the male gaze. Dwelling on humans unfortunately means Optimus and Megatron (Hugo Weaving) don’t appear until an hour in, and Megatron is not an active threat until the movie is nearly over. Speaking of Megatron, Weaving is nothing impressive. If they brought back Frank Welker, who voiced Megatron in G1 to pair with Cullen’s Optimus, it may have been more believable that these two had history. Weaving can act, he was good as Red Skull, but he can’t really in this movie. Speaking of the actual Transformers, Bumblebee having no lines gives him no character and we also don’t see him take the form of the 2007 Camaro. Jazz dying without any investment in his character is straight up shrewd. So now I’ve gotten past the problems with the characters. Does that mean the story’s good? I wish the answer was “Yes”. First, revisionist history opens a flood of confusion. The Hoover Dam was built due to the Cube (and the AllSpark) being there? And the two worlds have met before? So why then do the humans pretend they don’t know what’s happening? If none of the revisionist history was here and the events of the movie were the first time Cybertron’s inhabitants met humans on Earth, it would be a much cleaner story. Second, it takes too long to get to what really matters. It takes like 45 minutes to an hour to get to what matters, the Decepticons want the Cube and the Autobots can’t let that happen. Because of the human stuff, it prevents us from just cutting to the chase. Overall, a first entry that could have been worse, but does not provide encouragement for what’s next. 3/10 or 1½ stars.

texto: 2.5/10 "The first Transformers is actually kinda good." That's a sentence I've heard loads of times. I have no idea what's going on in the minds of the people who say that. The first Transformers is one of the most embarrassing AAA productions I know of. And it only goes downhill from here. The entire movie's attitude is just loathsome. It tries to mash a few dark and serious elements together with dialogue and comic relief straight out of a frat house. Every character is unbelievably obnoxious. I don't understand why anyone would ever want to follow these people, or why anyone would ever care about anything that's happening. The entire world this film takes place in is insufferable, and the whole thing feels like it was made by a bunch of college jocks. Everything about it is just annoying. It's also weird how often the movie seems to be attempting some kind of parody of the American government. The directing is actually okay for a production like this. The blend of on-set footage and CGI works great, and Bay directs the actors competently. What I do find hilarious, however, is just how clearly his background in music video directing shines through in quite a few shots. That - and especially how aggressively everything is geared towards being cool and badass - comes off as incredibly cringe and try-hard. Ninety per cent of the story is made up of some lame McGuffin fetch quest with stakes I couldn't care less about, because the world and the characters suck. And it all eventually culminates in one of the least exciting third acts I've ever seen. There's battle scene after battle scene, but not only do I barely know what's going on because half the Transformers look the same, I also don't really care. It's just more and more fighting, and I realised that watching Transformers transform into and out of cars had already gotten boring the third time around. This film is filled to the brim with stupid shit and is, in general, one of the most unenjoyable ways to spend two hours and fifteen minutes that I can think of.

texto: “Transformer” I know these movies are really popular from my generation but I’ve actually never watched any of the Michael Bay Transformers movies before in my life. Nor do I really care about this franchise. I haven’t even watched any Transformers cartoons when I was a kid. I owned no Transformers toys aside from some  Happy Meal toys. So I know virtually nothing about this series. Anyway watching this movie, it probably was a lot like the Michael Bay Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles movies I don’t know anything about Transformers so I can’t confidently say that but that’s definitely the vibe I got with this movie. The movie is actually pretty fun whenever the Transformers were on the screen, however that barely happened most of the movies does Shia LaBeouf and Megan Fox dicking around. Just like how most of Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles (2014) was just Megan Fox trying to get a news story and barely had the title characters in the movie. Same thing here I think it takes like over 50 minutes before we even see a transformer on screen. The movie was actually fun whenever we got to see them transforms especially when they’re in fights but whenever it’s Shia LaBeouf bitching about high school it got pretty annoying and pretty boring. This movie should be nonstop Transformers action but now we had to squeeze in Shia LaBeouf and Megan Fox in here. I mean at least I like that shot of Megan Fox over the hood of the car I think we’re gonna agree that shot define a generation of boys. Yeah I was not really much as the rest of the movie is pretty boring. If there’s not a transformer on the screen the movie is painfully boring, even the human action stuff like whenever we see the military guys go to war even that stuff pretty boring uninteresting. I like the one guy who was wearing a Redskins jersey for the entire movie, not cause I liked his character or found him interesting or anything. I just like seeing Redskins merch in media cause it’s a reminder that no matter how hard the NFL tries they’re not gonna erase the Redskins from history. But not much to say this is barely a Transformers movie. I wasn’t watching the sequel but no for when I heard this is the best one out of all five. Maybe I’ll check out “Rise Of The Beast”

texto: The transformers are not cool at all. The transformations are kinda cool I guess, but they only happen like three times. All of the transformers are not in it nearly enough. texto: An engaging blockbuster overall, but definitely one that loses itself its the final act. Starting off with its thrilling political intrigue, espionage, and military action, Transformers hooks you from the start with its brisk pace. LaBeouf is brilliant as Sam, flawlessly conveying his nerdy and comedic traits. The CGI’s thoroughly impressive, though they lack the holistic perspective of later films (not exactly a flaw). The character designs are brilliant (save perhaps Megatron), with the original lineup of Autobots and Decepticons being highly distinct from their respective groups. The action is fun for the most part, but certainly not as innovative or prominent as in later instalments. While Bumblebee received a major focus, I certainly wish Optimus had more screen time. Unfortunately, flaws are prevalent in the film’s middle and final acts. The Autobots hiding outside Sam’s home is cute at first, but quickly becomes obnoxious. The initial sequences with Sector 7 are largely uninteresting, hindering the previously thrilling pace. As for the final act, action sequences with the actual Transformers are brief. The overall resolution is abrupt, with Megatron feeling dumbed down for the sake of it. Still iconic, but lacks the action the Bayverse is known for. I don’t know how, but the military propaganda in Bay’s initial trilogy just works. And that ending scene is just legendary

texto: "I am Optimus Prime, and I send this message to any surviving Autobots taking refuge among the stars. We are here. We are waiting". Desde su creación Optimus Prime en toda adaptación, su liderazgo se basa en la responsabilidad, la empatía y la protección de aquellos que no pueden defenderse por sí mismos, Optimus ni siquiera busca el gobernar, sino preservar la libertad incluso en medio de una guerra. En contraste, Megatron encarna una búsqueda de poder que transforma el conflicto en una lucha cada vez más destructiva. Los humanos, por otro lado, constantemente intentan comprender, controlar o utilizar aquello que desconocen, especialmente cuando perciben una posible ventaja militar. Esta diferencia plantea una crítica interesante: una civilización tecnológicamente avanzada no necesariamente es una civilización moralmente superior. Aunque su guión puede resultar sencillo, la película consigue transmitir una sensación constante de caos, velocidad y capacidad de asombrarte por los efectos especiales.

texto: It’s been nearly 20 years since Transformers first released in theatres and I would still say that this is some of the best CGI to ever grace our screens. It’s honestly a cinematic feat. The movie has its own issues, like the hypersexualization of the female teenage lead, but I was honestly impressed at how well it held up upon rewatch. The sound design is incredible and makes every fight sequence feel so epic. Flawless pacing that takes its time to introduce vital characters instead of dropping you right into the action. The score and soundtrack is just so fantastic and so much fun. The final monologue playing out into Linkin Park’s “What I’ve Done”? Cinema!

texto: It’s been nearly 20 years since Transformers first released in theatres and I would still say that this is some of the best CGI to ever grace our screens. It’s honestly a cinematic feat. The movie has its own issues, like the hypersexualization of the female teenage lead, but I was honestly impressed at how well it held up upon rewatch. The sound design is incredible and makes every fight sequence feel so epic. Flawless pacing that takes its time to introduce vital characters instead of dropping you right into the action. The score and soundtrack is just so fantastic and so much fun. The final monologue playing out into Linkin Park’s “What I’ve Done”? Cinema!

texto: An engaging blockbuster overall, but definitely one that loses itself its the final act. Starting off with its thrilling political intrigue, espionage, and military action, Transformers hooks you from the start with its brisk pace. LaBeouf is brilliant as Sam, flawlessly conveying his nerdy and comedic traits. The CGI’s thoroughly impressive, though they lack the holistic perspective of later films (not exactly a flaw). The character designs are brilliant (save perhaps Megatron), with the original lineup of Autobots and Decepticons being highly distinct from their respective groups. The action is fun for the most part, but certainly not as innovative or prominent as in later instalments. While Bumblebee received a major focus, I certainly wish Optimus had more screen time. Unfortunately, flaws are prevalent in the film’s middle and final acts. The Autobots hiding outside Sam’s home is cute at first, but quickly becomes obnoxious. The initial sequences with Sector 7 are largely uninteresting, hindering the previously thrilling pace. As for the final act, action sequences with the actual Transformers are brief. The overall resolution is abrupt, with Megatron feeling dumbed down for the sake of it. Still iconic, but lacks the action the Bayverse is known for. I don’t know how, but the military propaganda in Bay’s initial trilogy just works. And that ending scene is just legendary

texto: Absolutely a propaganda movie about the US military, but it’s so worth the watch. Transformers (2007) is one of those movies that the whole family can enjoy. Action, comedy, romance, it has everything. Shia LaBeouf has a career defining performance as Sam. He’s smart, funny, and logical. At first it seems he’s a basic nerd who wants the girl, but he is shown to be witty and sincere. In the ocean of solid performances, there are a few that reach his watchability. Omar Benson Miller bashing through the glass window and getting tackled into the pool. Anthony Anderson and the donuts. Josh Duhamel as a stereotypical but affable soldier. Kevin Dunn and Julie White as probably the most enjoyable movie parents I’ve ever seen. And of course, Peter Cullen (rip) as the infamous Optimus Prime. This movie lays a foundation of a trilogy that would rock the late 2000’s family living room. Also, for me, this put Linkin Park on the map of everyone else who wasn’t already fans of the band. Michael Bay nails this movie in the most Michael Bay way.

texto: I was very shocked by the way the film ended because I was not expecting the story to take the direction that it did. After Madeleine supposedly committed suicide, John became obsessed with her and was unable to move on. When Judy came into his life, he wanted to change everything about her so that she would resemble Madeleine. Eventually, John took Judy back to the bell tower where Madeleine had “died” , the reason why he took Judy there was because he wanted to relive what had happened and become the hero he was not able to be the first time. Judy was scared and upset about being there, but John was determined to make it to the top. Once they reached the top of the bell tower, Judy became startled when she saw a shadowy figure and backed away and ended up falling to her death. I think the way that this movie was created was beautiful. There were a lot of colors, lighting, and sound effects that really stood out to me. For instance, when Judy is done with her makeover to look like Madeleine, there is a part where she steps out of the powder room and the lighting changes. Judy looks sad at first, but then she starts to smile, while John looks at her almost like he is seeing the ghost of Madeleine. This scene stuck with me because the expressions of the characters, lighting, and the sound effects, make everything seem eerie and unsettling. I think that this film is important to film studies because of the cinematography, along with the psychological effects that it produces. For instance, the obsession that John has with trying to make Judy more like Madeleine is quite alarming and can make for an interesting topic in studies.

texto: Coming out of Rear Window , my expectations for Hitchcock were that this would be a small, yet creatively-shot movie. Instead, it was massive, intricate, and impressive from all filmmaking standpoints—until its throwaway of an ending. Vertigo was a dark and complex story which keeps its audience on edge and guessing as there is never a moment where at least one of its characters isn’t going insane. It’s not a simple story with simple characters like Rear Window , and it definitely doesn’t leave anyone with a good feeling. The tricks that Hitchcock used to make some of the sequences magnificent are incredible to learn about, and the visuals—whether they be the stunning, colorfully-charged cinematography or the masterworks of 1950s editing that makes us feel uncomfortable yet fill us with wonder at the same time, this is a journey. The pure intention behind the focuses and the frames and even the shapes leave the viewer with a lot to dissect, until the ending discourages everything. This film was written incredibly well and its plot twist was a genuine shock. It felt like, through all its twists and turns, it was building up to a magnificent crescendo, but instead, its ending seemed to forget everything about the movie. Sure, it may seem like poetic justice, but that doesn’t change the fact that it didn’t make sense. Hitchcock impressed me with Vertigo, but I left frustrated as all the bells and whistles and hooks didn’t pay off in the end. For a journey of all sorts that never finds its destination, watch Vertigo. For a simple yet satisfying story, watch Rear Window .

texto: I jumped at the opportunity to see a Hitchcock that I'd never seen before at one of my local cinemas. I love 'Rope' and 'Rear Window', so hearing that 'Vertigo' is one of Hitchcock's masterpieces seemed like a no-brainer. To discover that it's actually one of most overrated films ever made was a bit upsetting to say the least. We all left the cinema with a sour taste in our mouths, wishing we could get out $16 back and that someone had told us the truth: 'Vertigo' actually kind of sucks. Hitchcock: the master of suspense. Little to no suspense in the whole film. What makes many of his other films great is that we as the audience know things that the characters don't. Never the case here. The pacing? Painfully slow and borderline unengaging. The twist was apparent from halfway through the film, so the second half was just enduring one sad and tiresome display of misogyny after another. How Jimmy Stewart became such a popular heart-throb in the 40s-60s is beyond me. He just mostly plays unlikable assholes that somehow women still like. Plenty of people seem to say how gorgeous this film looks as well. The depiction of San Francisco, the bright colours, and the one major dream sequence stand out of bold and expressive. Yet, so much of the film is also filmed in bland locations, with uninspired set-pieces and straight-forward blocking. I wasn't nearly as impressed as I expected to be. Then, to wrap everything up. The ending is terrible, with no sense of mystery or closure to hold onto, just a sad dead-end with no real enjoyment or satisfaction. The entire second half is a painful ordeal. It's hard to believe I watched the same film that hundreds of thousands of men and women over the last 58 years have given 8/10, 9/10, or 10/10 reviews to, or called Hitchcock's masterpiece. A predictable, slow, stale, offensive and mostly just off-putting drag. Sad. 4/10

texto: Je suis franchement déçu par Vertigo. Je comprends totalement pourquoi le film est considéré comme un classique et je reconnais le talent d’Hitchcock dans la mise en scène, la photographie et l’ambiance, mais je n’ai jamais vraiment accroché. J’ai trouvé le film beaucoup trop lent et j’ai souvent eu l’impression qu’il ne se passait pas grand-chose. Le vertige de Scottie, qui semblait être un élément central au début, m’a finalement paru assez peu exploité. L’idée autour de Madeleine/Judy et l’obsession de Scottie sont intéressantes, surtout quand on comprend toute la manipulation, mais ça n’a pas suffi à me faire apprécier le film. Même la révélation finale m’a laissé assez froid. Je reconnais son importance et ses qualités cinématographiques, mais personnellement, je n’ai pas pris le plaisir que j’espérais devant ce film. Peut-être que je l’apprécierai davantage avec le temps, mais pour l’instant, grosse déception.

texto: I jumped at the opportunity to see a Hitchcock that I'd never seen before at one of my local cinemas. I love 'Rope' and 'Rear Window', so hearing that 'Vertigo' is one of Hitchcock's masterpieces seemed like a no-brainer. To discover that it's actually one of most overrated films ever made was a bit upsetting to say the least. We all left the cinema with a sour taste in our mouths, wishing we could get out $16 back and that someone had told us the truth: 'Vertigo' actually kind of sucks. Hitchcock: the master of suspense. Little to no suspense in the whole film. What makes many of his other films great is that we as the audience know things that the characters don't. Never the case here. The pacing? Painfully slow and borderline unengaging. The twist was apparent from halfway through the film, so the second half was just enduring one sad and tiresome display of misogyny after another. How Jimmy Stewart became such a popular heart-throb in the 40s-60s is beyond me. He just mostly plays unlikable assholes that somehow women still like. Plenty of people seem to say how gorgeous this film looks as well. The depiction of San Francisco, the bright colours, and the one major dream sequence stand out of bold and expressive. Yet, so much of the film is also filmed in bland locations, with uninspired set-pieces and straight-forward blocking. I wasn't nearly as impressed as I expected to be. Then, to wrap everything up. The ending is terrible, with no sense of mystery or closure to hold onto, just a sad dead-end with no real enjoyment or satisfaction. The entire second half is a painful ordeal. It's hard to believe I watched the same film that hundreds of thousands of men and women over the last 58 years have given 8/10, 9/10, or 10/10 reviews to, or called Hitchcock's masterpiece. A predictable, slow, stale, offensive and mostly just off-putting drag. Sad. 4/10

texto: What a movie! For it being a psychological thriller, i think the giveaway of the plot twist happens way too soon. The only flaw for me is that we as viewers should have found out the twist along with Scottie. Other than that the movie is quite devastating. It’s about fear, obsession and how love can be and how it can take you to some really twisted places. I think it also shows how men can have this obsession with wanting something untouchable and fantasy-like, something they can’t have. The women other than Madeleine, Midge and Judy are both great women with good personalities who genuinely care for Scottie. Yet he seems to crave something that doesn’t make sense. His obsession with Madeleine is something you can’t really put a finger on. It also kind of shows how women are treated as desirable objects in the film and how they are desired only if they are a certain way. Anyway, lastly, the movie had very little to do with what “vertigo” actually is lol but regardless of that, it is a great movie!

texto: Alfred Hitchcock’s Vertigo reminds us that a movie, no matter the age, with a compelling story, engaging characters, and a genius use of visual techniques can create an entertaining cinematic experience. This movie shines in all these categories and, personally, has made this film a personal favorite of mine.  The first aspect of the film I really enjoyed was the emphasis on color as meaning. Hitchcock was a master at showing and not telling with a film, and this movie really proves that. The film’s Technicolor made Hitchcock’s storytelling through color really shine. You can tell when the film intends to invoke a certain idea or emotion, such as Madeleine’s silhouette shots with the green neon lights from the hotel sign illuminating the space. It seemed as though green invoked a sense of mystery to Madeleine’s character as Scottie slowly began to unravel the truth behind her aura. The color red also comes into play as it helps emphasize Scottie’s slow turn to obsession and lust for Madeleine’s image. The ultra-vibrant Red restaurant, a strong example of this technique, started to appear more frequently as Scottie began to spiral into psychological obsession. Another technique I really appreciated was the film’s pacing. Vertigo highlighted the importance of setting the plot with a slow start, and using that slow pace to parallel a sense of mystery and suspense. This film didn’t feed action in every scene; it kept the audience intrigued by creating a compelling case. The compelling Madeline case made me pay attention to the film even more, and as I realized, it surely rewarded me in the end with the movie’s signature twist. Pacing is really important because the more you pay attention, the more the film rewards you. To be honest, Vertigo did not challenge me in any of its aspects. Honestly, it was really refreshing watching a film that was slow and long because it helped me feel more connected to the story. This film did not feel forced or rushed; the unique story felt authentic to human experience. The psychological aspect of the film felt real because obsession, no matter what it can be about, could be experienced by anyone. With the success of the movie Obsession in 2026, I can see some similarities between both. Now, this doesn’t mean Vertigo Is the 1950s version of Obsession, but I can see some parallels between Bear’s character and Scottie's character. Both characters form a perfect image of their women, and with this obsession, slowly evolve from innocent loveable characters, to serious toxic individuals. After watching Obsession, I do have a better understanding of Vertigo. Watching Obsession helped me understand Scottie’s character on a much deeper level, especially because of the parallels with Bear. I could somehow know what Scottie was feeling and how his obsession would cause harm to his life after recalling what Bear went through in Obsession. In conclusion, Alfred Hitchcock’s Vertigo deserves to be recognized as a true classic. Its compelling, suspenseful, and rewarding story stands out among many modern films.

texto: I really enjoyed this movie because it was really interesting and mysterious. It really kept me thinking what would happen next and if Madeleine would ever notice him spying on her. When Madeleine died it really made me uneasy because Scottie become a new person and he really acted strangely, he forced Judy into becoming Madeleine which was just weird and I did not like that part of the movie. The colors were really vibrant in the movie, and it made me think what they could mean. When Scottie was in the restaurant seeing Madeleine for the first time the wall and floor was red which probably signified danger because ever since he started following her, his life just started going downhill. Her dress was green which represents mysteriousness which signifies that Madeleine is a mysterious person in the beginning of the movie because we knew nothing about her just that she goes into a trance from time to time. When Scottie had that dream and his face became green, I think they used that color to signify mysteriousness because he has never experienced that before until the death of “Madeleine.” All the colors in that sequence were just very unsettling because they were flashing and maybe meant danger or that he might lose his mind. The Camera shots were really good especially all the cinematic ones. One scene that really stood out to me was when they were at the church after Madeleine jumped off and Scottie was in the bottom right leaving the scene while the saints were climbing onto the roof and checking the body of Madeleine. I think this Scene really showed us the sense of fear that Scottie felt that he couldn’t stay there and talked to the saints who were checking. The Shots of the redwood forest really captivated me because it looked so beautiful and really wants me to go there and see them myself. Personally, I thought the beginning of the movie was really slow and kind of boring but ever since he talked to Gavin and made the plan to follow his wife that was when it really ramped up and it very interesting. It kind of made me reconsider my cardinal sin because I should be patient with movies because typically the beginning is always boring and slow but as it goes on it starts to get better. In conclusion for a movie that came out like 70 years ago it was really interesting and mysterious. I would definitely recommend this movie to some of my friends that aren’t in Film Arts and to my family.

texto: My Vertigo watching experience was magical but also intense at the same time.  The scene where Scottie was spying on Madeleine at the flower shop was a scene with breathtaking colors that caught my eye. I began to pay attention to the colors throughout the movie and I began to appreciate how much work the editors must've put. The colors especially at the flower shop created the illusion of a dream-like atmosphere and I couldn't help but to admire. During the confrontation between Scottie and Judy at the church, the camera was zoomed super close to both Judy's and Scottie's faces heightening the tension between the two. While watching the confrontation, I became super invested and I had forgotten about the slow-pacing of the first half of the movie. It was as if I was watching them argue in real time and the shadows and the music increased the intensity of that scene. All the comedic, intense, and romantic scenes were perfectly executed to the point where I wasn't mad that the movie was moving at a slower pace compared to modern movies. At first the slow-pacing was a drawback from my watching experience but all the camera angles, colors, and music compensated for a while. This was until we reached to the second half of the movie where Scottie saved Madeleine from drowning which where the movie got interesting. Everyone behind the scenes did a great job on this movie and in my opinion, Vertigo is a classic and this movie made me reconsider watching movies on my watch list that move at a slower pace.
